sens: Sow confusion and disorder in a group
Drive an army into disorganized flight
Disturb, agitate, vex
Destroy, annihilate
H2000.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of a violent and disorderly movement: creating chaos, noise, confusion. It is to put something or someone into a state of deep turmoil, as the Lord does to the Egyptians in Exodus 14:24, when He "puts their camp in disorder" at dawn.
2. In a wartime context, the word specifically refers to the action of throwing an enemy army into rout, that is, breaking it and scattering it in flight. This is what happens in Joshua 10:10: "The Lord put them to rout before Israel."
3. The word can also express inner turmoil, an agitation of the soul: in 2 Chronicles 15:6, God "stirs up" the peoples with anxieties, creating an atmosphere of fear and confusion.
4. Sometimes, the effect of this confusion is complete annihilation: in Deuteronomy 2:15, the hand of the Lord "destroys" the rebels in the camp, the word emphasizing that this rout leads to destruction.
H2000.origine: The Hebrew verb הָמַם comes from a root expressing tumultuous movement, noise, and disorderly agitation. The word evokes the physical image of chaos: people moving in all directions, disorder, noisy confusion. This notion of "making noise" while moving chaotically naturally extends to the meaning of "disturb" or "put to flight."
H2000.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and the Psalms. It is regularly used to describe divine intervention in battles: the Lord "puts to rout" the enemies of Israel through wonders (thunder in 1 Samuel 7:10, lightning in Psalms 18:15). The word also applies to situations of internal turmoil, as in 2 Chronicles 15:6 where anxieties "stir up" the peoples. Sometimes it approaches the meaning of pure destruction (Deuteronomy 2:15). The basic notion — creating chaos, disorder, a disorganized flight — is maintained in all these uses.
H2000.portee: This word reveals how the Bible understands divine intervention in history: God does not act through brute force, but by causing confusion, turmoil, and fear among the enemies of Israel, rendering them incapable of defending themselves. It is a lesson on the nature of divine victory: it often comes through psychological and strategic reversal rather than sheer power. For the believer, this word reminds us that in the face of obstacles, God can sow trouble among the adversary.

sens: minister of King Ahasuerus during the exile and return of Israel
mortal enemy of the Jews who plotted their destruction
man driven by limitless pride and ambition
person whose death plans turn against him
H2001.detail:
1. Haman is the chief minister ("vizier") of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) during the exile of the Jews in Persia, first mentioned in Esther 3:1. The king elevated him to power and placed him above all his officials.
2. He becomes the relentless enemy of the Jews, particularly of the Jew Mordecai who refused to bow down to him. He plotted to destroy the entire Jewish people in the provinces of the king (Esther 3:6), paying a large sum to the royal treasury for this purpose (Esther 3:11).
3. His pride and ambition are excessive: he boasted of his wealth, his many sons, and his power (Esther 5:11), but he could not tolerate that Mordecai did not rise before him. This anger against one man drove him to want to annihilate an entire people.
4. His death plot turned against him: exposed by Esther before the king, he was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7:10), and his house was given to Esther (Esther 8:1-2).
H2001.origine: The name means "magnificent" or "noble." Haman was the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, suggesting an origin in the ancient people of the Amalekites, hereditary enemies of Israel. This genealogy is not insignificant: it marks Haman as the spiritual heir of an ancient hostility toward the people of God.
H2001.emploi: Haman appears 48 times in the book of Esther, primarily in chapters 3 to 9. The narrative first shows him in a position of absolute power, receiving from the king the authorization to destroy all the Jews. His appearances alternate between moments of triumph (after obtaining the decree, when he joyfully leaves the royal feast) and moments of progressive humiliation (when he must honor Mordecai, when Esther identifies him as guilty). His ten sons are mentioned in Esther 9:7-9. The book of Esther reports his downfall and that of his house as the fulfillment of God's divine deliverance of the threatened Jewish people.
H2001.portee: The story of Haman illustrates the power of one who stands against the people of God and the divine reversal of his plans. It reveals that human pride, even when supported by political power, is fragile before God's Providence. For the Christian reader, Haman embodies the type of the enemy of faith whose schemes turn against him, and serves as a reminder that God watches over His people, even in exile and apparent absence.

sens: Chain or precious ornament worn around the neck
Insignia of dignity or royal distinction
H2002.detail:
1. The word refers to an ornamental object, generally made of gold or precious metals, worn around the neck. It is a necklace in the literal sense, a chain or piece of jewelry. In the story of Daniel, the king of Babylon offers a gold necklace to anyone who can read the mysterious inscription on the palace wall (Daniel 5:7).
2. The necklace is not just a simple ornament: it is a symbol of dignity and royal reward. When the king places a gold necklace around Daniel's neck (Daniel 5:29), he confers honor and authority upon him — it is a visible sign that the king distinguishes him among others and considers him worthy of power. The necklace accompanies the purple robe and the promise of the third highest position in the government.
H2002.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of hanging or suspending around the neck. In biblical Hebrew, this word belongs to the vocabulary of adornments and insignia of distinction, particularly used in contexts of court and royal dignity. It is a specifically Babylonian or Eastern-influenced word, reflecting the customs of the ancient Near East.
H2002.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in chapter 5 of Daniel, which recounts the fall of Babylon under Belshazzar. King Nebuchadnezzar first offers a gold necklace to anyone who can decipher the mysterious writing that appeared on the palace wall (Daniel 5:7). After Daniel presents himself, the king reiterates the same promise (Daniel 5:16): purple, gold necklace, and third dignity. Finally, when Daniel interprets the enigmatic words and announces the king's downfall, he keeps his word and indeed adorns Daniel with the gold necklace (Daniel 5:29). In all cases, the necklace is associated with honor, royal reward, and recognition of exceptional authority or wisdom.
H2002.portee: This word reminds us of a profound biblical truth: true dignity does not come from worldly ornaments or titles. Daniel receives the gold necklace from the king, but it is his faithfulness to God and his divine wisdom that earn him this honor. For the believer, this illustrates how God elevates His own and how the world ultimately recognizes those who serve Him with integrity, even in the most difficult or foreign circumstances.

sens: wood or twigs that are dried and easily flammable
that which burns quickly in fire
H2003.detail: 1. The word refers to very dry wood, twigs, or small branches that ignite easily. It is the ideal fuel for a quick fire. In Isaiah 64:1, the prophet asks God to come down "like a fire of dry wood": the image evokes a sudden and spectacular divine intervention. 2. By extension, dry wood symbolizes that which is consumed in an instant by fire, that which disappears without resistance. The same biblical image suggests God's transformative power in the face of obstacles: everything burns up like dry wood in His presence.
H2003.origine: The Hebrew word hemès (dry wood) comes from a root that expresses the idea of dryness, loss. In the Old Testament, it belongs to the lexical field of that which is dried up, fragile, ready to disappear. The image of dry wood catching fire is classic in poetic literature to evoke the speed and irresistibility of an action.
H2003.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 64:1. The prophet Isaiah uses it to describe how God should intervene: with the suddenness and power of fire igniting in dry wood. It is a poetic image of theophany, a fearsome manifestation of God to the nations. The rarity of the word emphasizes its effect: it is a touch of prophetic art that strikes the reader's imagination.
H2003.portee: For the believer, this image of dry wood catching fire reminds us that God can intervene with lightning speed, that nothing can resist His power. It invites us not to doubt His authority or His ability to transform situations, even the most stagnant. It is a comforting word in affliction and a call to fear God with respect.

sens: Look! See what is before you or what has just happened.
Solemn announcement: I am going to tell you something important.
Hypothetical condition: if, in case.
Affirmation of presence: here I am, there he is.
H2005.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to draw attention to something that appears or changes. "Behold, the man has become like one of us" (Genesis 3:22) refers to the moment when God points out the new condition of Adam and Eve after their sin. It is a gesture of the word that says "look, it has happened".
2. To announce what will follow, what one is about to reveal or do. "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8): God prepares the listener to hear a crucial choice. The word creates a solemn pause.
3. To express a condition or supposition, often nuanced by context: "If you had listened to me" or "Since". In 1 Samuel 12:3, "Here I am" also means "I present myself to be judged".
4. To affirm one's own presence or that of another at the moment of speaking: to respond to a call. Samuel responds "Here I am" to God (1 Samuel 3:4-8): he manifests, he is there, available.
H2005.origine: The Hebrew word הֵן (hen) is a simple and ancient interjection, a cry of attention. It has no "root" in the grammatical sense: it is a primary call word, like a pointing finger in language. It is found throughout the biblical text, from the Pentateuch to the prophets. It is distinct from other markers of attention like "oh" or "ah", but shares with them the function of capturing the listener's attention before an announcement.
H2005.emploi: The word הֵן appears about 310 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in narrative and prophetic contexts. It is encountered as early as Genesis (in the words of God, Abraham, Jacob) and in all historical and wisdom books. It carries several nuances: in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), "behold" often introduces a judgment or solemn promise; in personal dialogue (1 Samuel 3), it expresses the response of one who submits to the divine call; in narratives, it marks a turning point, a moment where something changes or must be noticed. It is one of the most common words in biblical Hebrew.
H2005.portee: This word teaches us to listen: it pauses the text and invites us to pay attention to what God or an important person says. For the believing reader, "behold" often signals a decisive moment — a promise, a judgment, a revelation. When we hear this word while reading the Bible, it is an invitation not to let it pass: something serious is being said. It is also the word of submission ("here I am"): one who responds "behold" presents themselves, surrenders, becomes available for what is to come.

sens: condition or hypothesis introducing an alternative
indirect inquiry about the existence or reality of something
H2006A.detail:
1. The word introduces a condition: "if you do this, then this will happen." It states a hypothesis and its possible consequences. In Ezra 4:13, the king states: "if this city is rebuilt and if its walls are raised, they will not pay tribute or tax"—this is a clearly posed condition.
2. The word can also express an indirect inquiry: "see if this is so" or "check if such a thing exists." In Ezra 5:17, one asks the king to investigate "if there was an order from Cyrus"—it is not about setting a condition, but about verifying an uncertain reality.
H2006A.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root (Aramaic is the language spoken by the Jews after the exile to Babylon) meaning "to look, to see." The Hebrew word hen (הֵן), from which the Aramaic form derives, is the exclamation "behold!" or "look!"—the idea is to draw attention. Over time, this word has shifted to a more abstract and logical meaning: to express a hypothesis or a question about what one will see or discover.
H2006A.emploi: The word appears 11 times, only in the Aramaic passages of the Bible: the book of Ezra (chapters 4 and 5) and the book of Daniel (chapters 2, 3, 5). These passages date from the post-exilic period when Aramaic was used. Generally, hen introduces a condition ("if you do this...") presenting two possible paths and their outcomes: in Daniel 2:5-6, Nebuchadnezzar threatens the Chaldeans "if you do not tell me the dream, you will be cut to pieces; but if you tell me, you will receive gifts." Sometimes, in passages of supposition or interpretation (like Ezra 5:17), the word marks uncertainty about a factual question.
H2006A.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible, written in several languages, reflects the real history of God with His people: Aramaic indicates contact with the Babylonian empire and the survival of Jewish faith in exile. On a logical and spiritual level, hen shows us how reasoning by conditions and consequences appears in biblical dialogues: Nebuchadnezzar and his servants reason by posing clear alternatives, inviting reflection. For the reader, it is an invitation to perceive the stakes of choices—obedience or disobedience, seeking or refusing the truth.

sens: marks a consequence or logical deduction
introduces an exhortation or advice that follows
expresses the reason for a request
H2006B.detail:
1. The word indicates that a conclusion follows from what precedes: a logical consequence. In Daniel 2:6, the king says to the magicians, "you will receive gifts and rewards from me... therefore tell me the dream" — the promised gift is the reason for his request.
2. It often introduces advice or an exhortation based on what has just been observed. In Daniel 4:27, the prophet says to the king, "therefore may my advice please you": he draws from the observation of the king's sin an exhortation to repentance.
3. Sometimes it emphasizes the reason for a question or an urgent request. In Daniel 2:9, the king repeats, "therefore tell me the dream" — he returns to his request as an inevitable conclusion of what has just been presented.
H2006B.origine: This Aramaic word is related to the Hebrew "lâhen" (לָהֵן, H3860), which serves the same function as a linking particle. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of direction, of moving from one point to another: the word "therefore" carries within it this image of transition, from the known to the unknown, from cause to effect.
H2006B.emploi: The word appears three times in the book of Daniel, in chapters 2 and 4. It is used in the mouth of King Nebuchadnezzar addressing the magicians and the prophet Daniel, to introduce his requests or exhortations. Each time, it links a request or advice to what precedes: a promise of reward, a threat of punishment, or the acknowledgment of a fault. It is a transitional word that structures the king's argumentation.
H2006B.portee: This small word shows how logic and reason lead to action. When the king understands something, he immediately draws a consequence: "therefore, do this." It is a lesson for the believer: grasping God's will requires not only intellect but also the decision and obedience that follow.

sens: personal pronoun referring to one or more women (or a mixed group)
personal pronoun referring to one or more things, abstract or concrete realities
marker of copula or identity between two realities
H2007.detail:
1. This word is the feminine form of the pronoun "he/she" in Hebrew. When the text speaks of women or a group in the feminine, it uses this pronoun to say "they" (in a feminine context). For example, in Exodus 1:19, the midwives respond to Pharaoh: "they give birth before the midwife arrives," where "they" refers to "the Hebrew women."
2. This pronoun is also used to refer to things — objects, events, concepts. In Proverbs 6:16, the Lord hates "six things": here, the text uses this word to refer to those enumerated realities.
3. The word can also play the role of a small particle that links or identifies two elements: it is a very Hebrew usage where this word means "it is," "they are." In Leviticus 18:17, "These are your close relatives": the word indicates that this kinship link is established.
H2007.origine: This word comes from the root of the fundamental pronoun hu (הוּא), which means "he," "she," "it." Henah is its plural feminine form or an emphatic variant. It is a very ancient pronoun, present since the beginnings of the Hebrew language, which simply expresses identification or reference to a being or thing already mentioned.
H2007.emploi: This word appears 28 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narrative prose of the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It refers back to feminine subjects or groups of things: women (Genesis 6:2, Exodus 1:19), cities (Jeremiah 34:7, Ezekiel 30:17), abstract realities (Proverbs 6:16). Its usage is purely grammatical: it simply links the discourse by referring back to what precedes, or it establishes an identity ("they are"). The text renders it variously in English depending on the context: "they," "these," "they are."

sens: in this place where I am, where you are, or where one speaks
toward this place, in this direction
at this moment, now
in this circumstance, in this state of affairs
H2008.detail:
1. The most common meaning is spatial: "here" designates the present or nearby place, the one where the speaker or the one being spoken to is located. Samson arrived "here" in Gaza (Judges 16:2): it is in the city where he is. David says to his father, "come down here as soon as possible" (Genesis 45:13): he invites him to come to the place where he is in Egypt.
2. The word can also express movement toward a place, the idea of "come here" or "go there." When it says, "they passed here and there" (2 Kings 2:8), the double usage shows the character of dispersion: here and there, everywhere.
3. Sometimes the word is used to indicate the present moment, "now" or "at present." It emphasizes what is happening at this precise moment in the narrative.
4. In other contexts, "here" takes on a figurative meaning: the current state of affairs, the present situation. The iniquity of the Amorites "is not yet complete" (Genesis 15:16): the word expresses the idea of completeness, of a point of culmination reached at this moment.
H2008.origine: The Hebrew adverb הנה (hennah) is formed from the root "hn" which expresses presence and proximity. It is related to הן (hen), "behold" or "look," which introduces what is visible or present. The word fundamentally expresses the idea of pointing out: "look there, this is here." In Hebrew, it is a very common word to designate the space and time of the speaker.
H2008.emploi: This word appears 41 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the prophets. It is one of the simplest and most commonly used adverbs. In the narratives, it creates an effect of immediacy: "Samson arrived here" (Judges 16:2) places the reader on site. Often it marks invitation, command, or exhortation: "Come here," "Look here." In some figurative passages (Genesis 15:16, Proverbs 9:4), it extends to the meaning of "now" or "completeness": the action or state being discussed concentrates at the moment or point being discussed. Its usage remains very natural and concrete.
H2008.portee: This small word reminds us that the Bible is a living and spoken narrative. The frequent use of "here" creates proximity: the reader is invited to place themselves in the scene, to see and hear. It is a subtle stylistic means that makes the words of God and the patriarchs not distant and abstract, but present and addressed. The word invites attention: "Listen here, look here" — it is the emphasis of one who has something important to communicate.

sens: Draws attention to something that is present or has just occurred
Introduces an important statement or an event about to happen
Marks surprise or astonishment at a sudden reality
Emphasizes an assertion or a factual observation
H2009.detail:
1. The word calls the reader or listener to look at or observe something immediate and visible: "Behold the man of whom I spoke to you" (1 Samuel 9:17), where Samuel shows Saul to David. It is a gesture of direct designation.
2. It announces the arrival of an important event or a solemn word from God: "Behold, I give you every herb that yields seed" (Genesis 1:29) opens God's gift to humanity. It is a major introductory formula.
3. It expresses the sudden discovery of a reality that is often unexpected or striking: "Behold, this also is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 2:1), where the wise man observes with astonishment that even joy remains vain.
4. It punctuates a divine assertion or promise to underscore its importance and certainty: "Behold, the Lord passed by" (1 Kings 19:11) marks the decisive moment when God reveals Himself to Elijah.
H2009.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "seeing" and "making see." The form "hinneh" is an imperative that literally means "make see" or "look." It is a very ancient term, present throughout the Old Testament, belonging to the solemn and direct language of divine revelation. It appears particularly in moments when God shows Himself or makes Himself known to His servants.
H2009.emploi: This word is used about 800 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis and the prophetic books. It serves several purposes: announcing a divine manifestation (God says "Behold"), pointing to a present situation ("Behold the man"), marking a dramatic or revealing turning point. In Genesis, it punctuates the creation narrative and the patriarchs (Genesis 1:29, 6:12, 18:2, 22:11). In historical and prophetic accounts, it highlights decisive moments. Its meaning varies slightly: sometimes simple attestation ("he is there"), sometimes solemn call ("look closely"), but it always focuses attention on the essential.
H2009.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God speaks clearly and directly, without detour. Each biblical "Behold" invites us to see, to recognize God's action or the given word. It is an invitation to spiritual vigilance: to listen to what God designates, not to remain passive before His acts and promises. This word also teaches the importance of the present moment in God's plan.

sens: Cease from work, day of relaxation and celebration
Leave granted by authority to a population
Break, interruption of a usual activity
H2010.detail:
1. The word designates a cessation of work and relaxation, a moment when one stops usual activities to rest or celebrate. In Esther 2:18, King Ahasuerus "grants rest to the provinces": he suspends the ordinary fiscal and administrative demands of the regions under his authority, offering a pause to the population in honor of his marriage to Esther. It is both a rest from labor and a gesture of royal generosity.
2. The word can more broadly refer to a break, an interruption of a burdensome activity or a tense situation. It evokes the idea of relief: one ceases to endure pressure, finding respite.
H2010.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to rest, to find rest." It is related to the image of rest as relief and natural pause after effort. The context of the passage in Esther shows that this rest can also be an official gesture, a grace granted by one who has authority.
H2010.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 2:18. King Ahasuerus grants rest to the provinces of his empire to celebrate his marriage to Esther. The use in this context of the Persian court shows that "rest" can mean not only a personal cessation of work but also an official release, a lightening of burdens imposed on a region. It is an act of royal favor towards the subjects.
H2010.portee: This word reminds the reader that rest is a precious gift, a relief granted by one who has authority. For the Christian, it evokes the rest promised in Christ (cf. Hebrews 4), a rest that is not only physical but spiritual, a deliverance from the bondage of sin and anxiety. The passage in Esther also shows that even in a pagan empire, God can influence the hearts of rulers to grant grace and relief to His people.

sens: Deep and narrow valley with rocky slopes, located southwest of Jerusalem
Valley that served as a boundary between the territories of the tribes of Israel
H2011G.detail:
1. The valley of Hinnom is a particular geographical formation: a deep and narrow depression carved between steep rocks, located southwest of Jerusalem. It separates Mount Zion to the north from the hill known as "the hill of iniquity" and the rocky plateau of the plain of Rephaim to the south. In Joshua 18:16, it appears as a visible landmark in the delineation of tribal boundaries, a place that stands out due to its distinctive shapes.
2. The valley of Hinnom served as a natural demarcation line between territories: it marked the boundaries between regions of Israel. This is why it appears in Nehemiah 11:30 as the extreme point of the territory recolonized after the exile, showing the extent of the territory reclaimed by the Israelites.
H2011G.origine: The name Hinnom means "lamentation" or "groaning" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a place where cries or weeping were heard. It is a proper name that appears in biblical texts to designate a well-identified geographical reality around Jerusalem. Later in biblical history, this place will take on a dark spiritual significance, particularly with its association with Topheth.
H2011G.emploi: The valley of Hinnom appears twice in the Hebrew Bible provided here, both times as a geographical marker in the delineation of boundaries. In Joshua 18:16, it is included in the description of the territory of Benjamin, one of the many boundaries established during the division of Canaan. In Nehemiah 11:30, it marks the southern limit of the area reclaimed after the Babylonian exile. In these two passages, it is a well-known valley, a natural feature of the terrain that the biblical writers use as a reference point to define specific areas of territory.
H2011G.portee: This valley reminds us how the geography of the promised land to Israel was concrete and memorable: the boundaries were not abstract, but inscribed in the land itself. It invites the reader to see the Promised Land not as an abstraction, but as a defined territory, given by God, of which each tribe receives its portion with visible landmarks.

sens: a valley southwest of Jerusalem, with rocky and steep sides
the place where offerings were burned to idols, including children
H2011H.detail:
1. Hinnom is a deep and narrow valley, with steep rocky walls, located southwest of Jerusalem. It borders Mount Zion to the north and extends toward the rocky plateau of the plain of Rephaim to the south. The land boundary accounts (Joshua 15:8 and 18:16) mention this valley as a geographical landmark that marks the borders of the lands conquered by Israel.
2. This valley becomes a place of religious abomination: several kings of Israel burn incense there and make their sons pass through the fire in honor of Molech, a foreign deity (2 Kings 23:10; 2 Chronicles 28:3 and 33:6). These practices are repugnant to the God of Israel and contradict His commandments. Jeremiah denounces these "high places" built at Topheth in the valley as the result of evil thoughts that God never commanded (Jeremiah 7:31).
H2011H.origine: The name Hinnom means "lamentation" or "groaning" in Hebrew. It most likely comes from the root that expresses a cry of pain. Hinnom was the name of a real valley near Jerusalem. Combined with Topheth (which refers to the hearth of sacrifices), this valley becomes in Scripture a symbol of divine judgment and destruction.
H2011H.emploi: The valley of Hinnom first appears as a concrete geographical landmark in the descriptions of the lands allocated to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 15 and 18). It then enters the narratives of the religious infidelities of certain kings: Ahaz, Manasseh, and others commit abominations there by sacrificing their children to idols (2 Kings 23:10; 2 Chronicles 28:3 and 33:6). The prophet Jeremiah uses this valley as an emblem of the coming judgment, transforming it from a physical place into an image of eternal punishment (Jeremiah 7:31-32; 19:2-6; 32:35). It thus becomes laden with negative spiritual connotations in biblical thought.
H2011H.portee: The valley of Hinnom reminds the believer how idolatry and rejection of divine will lead to increasingly grave abominations — even to the point of sacrificing one's own children. It shows that following foreign gods leads to spiritual destruction and judgment. For the New Testament reader, this valley should evoke the seriousness of rejecting God and the reality of future judgment.

sens: City in Mesopotamia conquered by the Assyrians
H2012.detail: 1. Héna is a city in the region of Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq), which was conquered and subdued by Assyrian kings before the time of Sennacherib. It is mentioned alongside other defeated cities — Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Ivva — that the Assyrian king lists to boast of his military victories (2 Kings 18:34). The fact that Héna is cited among these cities shows that it was significant enough to be a symbol of Assyrian power.
H2012.origine: The name Héna comes from Hebrew and refers to a historical city in Mesopotamia. Its etymological meaning evokes the idea of "troubling" or "agitating," an image that may reflect either political turbulence or the belligerent nature of the region. The city actually existed and was among the Assyrian conquests of the 8th century BC.
H2012.emploi: Héna appears three times in the Bible, always in the same context: the speech of the Assyrian king reported in 2 Kings 18:34 and 19:13, and then cited in the prophet Isaiah 37:13. The Assyrian king Sennacherib, besieging Jerusalem, lists the cities he has conquered to intimidate King Hezekiah by asserting: "Where are the gods of these cities? Could they save them?" Héna is included in this list of tributary or destroyed cities, serving as supposed proof of Assyrian omnipotence and the impotence of local gods.
H2012.portee: This proper name reminds the reader that earthly powers, however impressive they may seem, remain under God's control. The ironic enumeration of these defeated cities, far from impressing Hezekiah and the people of Judah, should lead them to trust in the Lord rather than in human alliances. It is an invitation not to fear military threats when seeking refuge in the true God.

sens: to silence, impose silence
to remain silent, say nothing
to refrain from speaking as a sign of respect or submission
H2013.detail:
1. To silence someone means to order or ask them to stop speaking. Caleb "silences" the people who are murmuring against Moses (Numbers 13:30); the king says "Silence!" to dismiss his courtiers (Judges 3:19). It is an action imposed from the outside.
2. To remain silent means to say nothing oneself, voluntarily or involuntarily. The Levites ask the people to be silent because the day is holy (Nehemiah 8:11): it is refraining from speech. In the house of mourning, one cries out "Silence!" because it is not the time to mention the name of the Lord (Amos 6:10).
3. Silence can be an act of respect or worship before God. "Let all the earth be silent before Him!" (Habakkuk 2:20): it is to be silent to listen, to acknowledge divine majesty. The corpses thrown in silence (Amos 8:3) evoke a silence of desolation.
H2013.origine: The original Hebrew root evokes the idea of ceasing noise, calming down. It produces the noun "silence" and the verb "to silence." In Greek, this word often corresponds to the verb "sigaô" (σιγάω), which carries the same idea: to impose or observe mutism. The basic image is that of noise coming to a stop.
H2013.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets and narratives. It is used both as a direct command ("Silence!") addressed to groups, and as a description of an attitude. In the narratives (Numbers, Judges, Nehemiah), it is a concrete action: to make words cease. In the prophets (Amos, Habakkuk), silence takes on a broader hue: the silence of desolation (Amos 8:3) or of worship (Habakkuk 2:20). The expression "to be silent" in Amos 6:10 and Habakkuk 2:20 marks a moment when human speech must fade away.
H2013.portee: Silence, in the Bible, is not an absence: it is an attentive presence. To be silent before God is to acknowledge His sovereignty and create space to listen to His voice. For the Christian, this invites examination of one's words: are they useful? Should one sometimes remain silent to respect the holiness of the moment or the person? Voluntary silence before God is an act of worship.

sens: absence d'activité ou de mouvement
arrêt ou interruption
soulagement temporaire de la peine ou de la fatigue
H2014.detail: 1. The word first denotes the absence of activity, the act of ceasing to do something: a pause, a stop in what was previously occupying. In Lamentations 3:49, the psalmist says that his eyes know no "relief" — they do not stop crying, there is no interruption to his tears. 2. By extension, it evokes the relief or relaxation that a pause brings: rest as a temporary easing of pain or fatigue. The context of Lamentations clearly shows this nuance: it is not simply a mechanical stop, but the absence of the relief that a pause would bring in the midst of distress.
H2014.origine: The Hebrew word הֲפוּגָה comes from a root meaning "to cease" or "to stop." It is constructed as a derived noun expressing the idea of interruption or cessation, close to the notion of suspending an action, from which the meaning of rest or calm naturally derives.
H2014.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 3:49. The psalmist expresses the unbroken continuity of his distress: without rest, without relief, his eyes flow with tears. This context shows that the word does not simply describe a physical pause, but the absence of any relief or easing in the face of deep and persistent suffering.
H2014.portee: This word reminds the reader that suffering without rest is a state that God knows and that the Bible acknowledges as real. It speaks to those who are going through unending distress, validating their experience and implicitly inviting them to seek in God alone the comfort that the world cannot offer.

sens: To topple or knock something from its state or position
To change the direction, orientation, or course of something
To modify, transform the nature or state of something
To become different, to transform
To go from prosperity to ruin or destruction
To act against someone, to turn against them
H2015.detail: 1. To overturn an object or structure: to make it fall, to knock down, to physically destroy. When the Lord "turned their waters into blood" (Psalms 105:29), the water is overturned from its natural state to become something else. 2. To turn in another direction: to orient differently, to change course. In Genesis 3:24, the flaming sword "turns" in all directions to guard the way. 3. To transform, to deeply modify: to change the very nature of something. Leprosy "becomes" (changes) the hair to white (Leviticus 13:20). 4. To transform oneself, to change state or condition: to become other than one was. Esther 9:22 speaks of a month that "changed" from mourning to joy. 5. To destroy, to annihilate: to reduce to nothing. Sodom was "destroyed" (Genesis 19:25) completely. 6. To turn against someone, to become hostile: to act in the opposite direction. "Against me he turns and turns his hand" (Lamentations 3:3) expresses God's hostility.
H2015.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of turning, toppling, turning upside down. The basic image is that of rotational movement or tipping: something that changes position or orientation. The word has several forms: the simple form (Qal) describes the action of turning or overturning, while other forms express passive or reciprocal transformation. This root belongs to the fundamental vocabulary of Hebrew to speak of change.
H2015.emploi: This verb appears 92 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical narratives, laments, and psalms. It first describes concrete actions: God overturns the walls of Jericho (Joshua), transforms water into blood (Exodus 7), overturns cities like Sodom. But it extends to the figurative: the change of intention or feeling (Deuteronomy 23:5, where God "turned" the curse into a blessing), spiritual transformation (1 Samuel 10:6, where the Spirit changes Saul), the reversal of fate (Esther 9:1, where the day intended for oppression "turned" for the Jews). The word can also express the destruction or ruin of a city or people.
H2015.portee: This word teaches us that God is the absolute master of change and overturning. Nothing is fixed or irreversible under His hand: He can transform a curse into a blessing, oppression into deliverance. For the believer, this speaks of hope: our situations can be "overturned" in our favor. But the word also carries a warning: the wicked will be overturned, the ungodly cities destroyed. It is a call to turn to God before He turns against us.

sens: That which opposes, which is the inverse of another thing
Behavior or attitude that goes against the norm or the expected
Obstinacy, refusal to follow the established order
H2016.detail: 1. The word designates that which directly opposes something else, the inverse or the opposite. In Ezekiel 16:34, the city of Jerusalem is described as being "the opposite" of other prostitutes: while women who prostitute themselves usually receive money from their clients, Jerusalem gives money to obtain lovers, completely overturning the usual logic. 2. The word also expresses a peculiarity, a behavior that deviates from the normal order of things. It is to act in a way contrary to what is expected or what others do. 3. By extension, it can denote a form of perversity or obstinacy, a deliberate will to do the opposite of what is right or proper.
H2016.origine: The Hebrew word הֶפֶךְ (hèphèkh) comes from the root חפך (h.ph.k) which means "to turn, to return, to overturn." This root evokes the image of something turned upside down, transformed, inverted. The same verb appears in Ecclesiastes and Proverbs to speak of change or reversal of situation. The image is one of inversion: instead of going in one direction, one goes in the other.
H2016.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 16:34. It is a passage where the prophet Ezekiel reproaches Jerusalem for its moral perversity. The city is compared to a woman who prostitutes herself, but in a perverted, inverted way: instead of receiving money like other prostitutes, she gives it. What is remarkable is that the prophet uses the word "opposite" to emphasize the absurdity and folly of Jerusalem's behavior. It is not merely infidelity; it is a ridiculous and self-destructive infidelity that shows the extent of its moral degradation.
H2016.portee: This word reminds us that sin is not only a transgression; it is also an inversion of the order that God has established. Jerusalem acts "in reverse," which makes its behavior not only wrong but absurd. For the Christian reader, this invites us to see sin as a form of folly: it claims to offer us something, but it ruins us. Recognizing our own "opposition" to God's ways is the first step toward repentance.

sens: distortion, overturning of the natural order
rebellious attitude that inverts just roles or relationships
mentality that contests legitimate authority
H2017.detail:
1. The word describes a distortion or an overturning: something that should go straight is twisted, something that should have a logical order is inverted. It is the image of something turned upside down. In Isaiah 29:16, the prophet denounces the perversity of those who say that the potter does not exist or lacks intelligence, thereby overturning the obvious relationship between the creator and the creature.
2. It is a deeply rebellious attitude, a mentality that opposes the order desired by God. It consists not only of bad acts but of a disposition of the heart that claims to invert true relationships: the creature stands against the creator, the servant against his master. This perversity of judgment leads to denying the obvious and failing to recognize the one who has authority over us.
H2017.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to turn," "to overturn," "to turn away." It evokes the image of something turned, of a path deviated from its natural direction, of an order upset. This root fundamentally expresses the opposite of straightness: not merely error, but the deliberate inversion or twisting of what should be straight.
H2017.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible (in Isaiah 29:16), making it a rare but powerful term. It is found in an oracle of the prophet Isaiah, who denounces the pride and blindness of a people who claim to govern themselves without God. The prophet qualifies this twisted judgment that inverts roles as "perversity": the potter should be recognized for his work, and the vessel has no reason to deny the one who shaped it. It is a perversity of judgment and thought, far more than a mere isolated moral fault.
H2017.portee: This word calls us to discern modern forms of perversity: that which denies the evidence that God created all things, that which overturns legitimate authorities, that which claims that the creator does not exist or lacks intelligence. Perversity is a voluntary blindness, a twisting of thought that hardens the heart. Recognizing the Creator is to emerge from this inversion and return to the true order.

sens: Total and sudden destruction of a place, city, or region
Cataclysm, complete annihilation resulting from divine intervention
Brutal overturning of the established order
H2018.detail:
1. The word refers to the complete and catastrophic destruction of the cities of the plain — Sodom, Gomorrah, and the surrounding cities — by the direct intervention of God. This event is presented as a total upheaval of these places: it is not only the death of their inhabitants but the annihilation of the very framework of their existence (Genesis 19:29).
2. The disaster evokes a sudden and irrevocable overturning: what was established, prosperous, inhabited, becomes ruin. The text shows that God "overturned" (the same root word) the cities, as if they were turned upside down, both in their physical reality and in their collective existence.
3. This word also carries the idea of divine judgment: the disaster is not a blind calamity, but the consequence of a higher will that punishes sin. It is an act of destruction that carries moral significance.
H2018.origine: The Hebrew word חֲפֵכָה (ha.phe.khah) comes from the root חפך (hpk), which means "to overturn," "to turn back," "to disturb." The same root produces verbs that describe physical turning or inversion of the order of things. It expresses the idea of tipping, radical and irreversible transformation. In biblical texts, this family of words is constantly associated with acts of divine destruction or catastrophic judgments.
H2018.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 19:29, where it specifically refers to the destruction of the cities of the plain by God. The context is that of divine judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah due to their grave sins. Although rare, this word plays a decisive role in this foundational narrative: it names the divine act of destruction that spares Lot (because of his connection to Abraham) but annihilates everything else. Its very uniqueness underscores the theological importance of this event as an archetype of irreversible divine judgment.
H2018.portee: This word reminds the believer that God does not indefinitely tolerate grave sin and idolatry: He is a God of justice who acts to destroy what opposes His holiness. At the same time, the context shows His mercy: He remembers His promises to Abraham and spares Lot. The disaster of the cities thus becomes a warning for every reader about the reality of divine judgment, tempered by the certainty that God protects His own.

sens: Who strays from the straight path
Who is twisted, bent
Who deviates from justice or moral uprightness
H2019.detail:
1. The word literally refers to what strays from the direct path: a road that zigzags, a path that does not go straight. It is the image of physical diversion.
2. Applied to behavior, it describes one who does not walk according to the straight line: someone whose ways are tortuous, unpredictable, diverted. In Proverbs 21:8, "the guilty follow diverted paths": the sinner does not walk straight ahead, he takes detours, avoiding clarity.
3. In a moral sense, the word expresses perversion, the voluntary deviation from what is just and right. It is the opposite of uprightness: a life twisted by sin, intentions curved rather than frank.
H2019.origine: The Hebrew word is formed by reduplication (hèpekh-pèkh): the same root repeated creates the idea of repeated twisting, a deviation that worsens. The root evokes the action of turning, returning, inverting. This repetition gives the word its strength: it is not only bent but resolutely diverted.
H2019.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 21:8, in the context of divine judgment on human ways. The wise man contrasts the guilty who "follow diverted paths" with the innocent who "acts with uprightness." This unique occurrence contrasts two life paths: that of the wicked, who seeks to hide and divert, and that of the righteous, who walks in full light. It is a classic image of biblical wisdom, where uprightness is the supreme virtue and diversion is the sign of sin.
H2019.portee: This word invites the reader to examine their own spiritual walk: am I in the straight paths of God, or are my intentions and actions diverted? Wisdom calls for transparency, frankness, and moral uprightness. Those who follow Jesus, who is "the way," renounce deceptive detours and walk in truth.

sens: Help that saves from danger, oppression, or death
Escape, way out in the face of a threat
Intervention of God to rescue His people from captivity or the enemy
H2020.detail: 1. Deliverance is a concrete help: it is the act of being saved from a desperate situation. In Esther 4:14, Mordecai tells Esther that if she does not speak to save the Jews from the extermination ordered by Haman, "relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place" — meaning that God will find a way to save His people, even without her. 2. The word evokes the idea of an escape, a way out in the face of danger: it is salvation that arrives when everything seems lost. 3. In the biblical tradition, deliverance is often the work of God: it is He who pulls His people from slavery, invasion, or persecution.
H2020.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root צלל (tsl), which means "to bend, to hide, to escape." The basic image is that of a fugitive who flees and hides. Deliverance is therefore literally "the action of escaping." The prefix ה- and the suffix -ה form a feminine noun, giving the root a substantive form that designates the act or state of being saved.
H2020.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 4:14, a key moment in the narrative: Esther is queen of Persia, her Jewish people face extermination, and Mordecai urges her to use her influence. The "deliverance" here is not automatic — it depends on human action (Esther must risk her life) and the providence of God. Mordecai expresses a certain faith: even if Esther refuses, God will save the Jews in one way or another. It is a rare but powerful word, concentrating all the hope of God's people in the face of annihilation.
H2020.portee: This word from Mordecai speaks to the heart: it reminds us that God never abandons His people, even on the brink of disaster. But it also places responsibility on Esther's shoulders — and thus on ours: God saves, but He invites us to act, to risk, to stand firm at the decisive moment. Deliverance is never pure passivity; it requires courage and faith.

sens: War equipment carried or wielded in battle
Set of weapons and armor available to an army
H2021.detail:
1. The word refers to a piece of war equipment used in battle, something that the warrior carries or holds to strike, protect, or fight. It is a concrete term that refers to the material weapons of the soldier.
2. In its biblical context, it is also used to refer to the entire military equipment of an army: weapons, armor, helmets, shields. In Ezekiel 23:24, the prophet enumerates the various weapons "with the great shield and the small shield, with helmets" to show the overwhelming power of the army advancing against Jerusalem.
H2021.origine: This Hebrew word designates the tools of war and violence. The text of Ezekiel shows a parallel use with "shield" and "helmet," confirming that the word covers all martial equipment — the offensive weapons and the defensive armor of the warrior.
H2021.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 23:24. The prophet uses it in a judgment speech against Jerusalem: he lists all the elements of the Babylonian warrior's equipment that are preparing to attack — chariots, wheels, shields, helmets, and "weapons." This military and imminent war context shows that the word designates the concrete equipment of the soldier marching into battle.
H2021.portee: This word reminds us that the power of armies and human weapons, however impressive it may seem, remains an earthly reality against which only God can grant or deny judgment and victory. For the believer, it invites us not to fear the threats of the powers of this world.

sens: Natural elevation of the terrain, higher than a hill, forming a barrier or refuge
Remarkable summit designated by a proper name, place of worship, meeting, or important event
Mountain range or massif
Mountainous region, land of mountains
Obstacle or difficulty overcome by faith or obedience
H2022G.detail:
1. The mountain is primarily a mass of land that rises high above the plains: it is the image of relief that dominates the landscape. During the flood, "all the high mountains that were under the whole heaven were covered" (Genesis 7:19), which shows how the water submerged the earth to the point of erasing even the greatest peaks.
2. Some mountains become sacred or historical places: Moses receives the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:2-20:18), Abram offers a sacrifice on the mountain that God designates (Genesis 22:2-14), and sacrifices to the Lord are celebrated on His mountain (Psalms 24:3).
3. The word also refers to chains or massifs: when Ezekiel describes a great fallen tree, "its branches fell in the mountains and in all the valleys" (Ezekiel 31:12), which evokes the extent of the rugged terrain.
4. An entire mountainous region can be called "mountain": Israel returns from the mountain of Gilead (Judges 7:3), which designates a whole country or mountainous region.
5. The mountain can metaphorically represent an obstacle, a challenge to overcome: who may ascend the mountain of the Lord? raises the question of access to His presence (Psalms 24:3), which implies a moral and spiritual ascent.
H2022G.origine: The Hebrew word har comes from a root that designates what rises, stands up towards the top. In Hebrew, words of the same family generally evoke the idea of eminence or height. This word is used throughout the Hebrew Bible to refer to both natural mountain ranges (such as Hermon or Ararat) and places where the divine manifests or where man encounters God, making it a key word in the landscape and biblical theology.
H2022G.emploi: The word har appears 402 times in the Old Testament, in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and the prophetic books. It primarily designates concrete geographical realities: the high mountains of the flood, Mount Hor, the mountains of the Sinai region. But it quickly acquires a religious significance: Sinai and Horeb are the mountains of divine revelation, where Moses receives the Law and where God manifests in fire and smoke. Abraham ascends Mount Moriah to offer a sacrifice in obedience to God. The psalms speak of "the mountain of the Lord" as the center of worship and sanctuary. In the prophets, mountains become images of stability, strength, or judgment. The word thus encompasses both the geographical and the theological.
H2022G.portee: The mountain reminds the believer of the majesty and power of God: the relief that no man has created testifies to the greatness of the Creator. It also symbolizes access to God — to ascend it is to seek His presence, His word, His covenant. The great acts of God (revelation, sacrifice, judgment) often take place on a mountain: it is there that the turning points of salvation history are decided. It finally teaches that faith must overcome obstacles and rise above fear and doubt to meet God.

sens: Natural elevation of the terrain, more or less high and steep
Mountainous region or hill, considered as a geographical area
Region, territory, or mountainous country
Natural refuge or elevated place to retreat
H2022H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a mountain or hill, a natural formation of the terrain that rises towards the sky. In Genesis 14:6, we speak of "the mountain of Seir," a true mountain range where the Horites lived.

2. More often, "mountain" describes an entire geographical region characterized by mountainous relief: the "mountain of Ephraim" (Joshua 20:7), the "mountain of Judah" (Joshua 20:7), or the "mountain of Naphtali" (Joshua 20:7) do not designate a single peak, but an entire region of Israel. It is an administrative and geographical term for the highlands.

3. This word also expresses the general idea of "high lands" or "hills" opposed to plains and valleys (Joshua 11:2: "the mountain, the plain south of Kinnereth"). It is an element of the landscape that structures the space.

4. Finally, the mountain is a place of refuge or retreat. In 1 Samuel 23:14, David stands "in the mountain of the wilderness of Ziph" to hide; in Judges 3:27, Ehud calls the people to rise "in the mountain of Ephraim" to gather away from danger.
H2022H.origine: The word הַר (har) is a very ancient root of Hebrew. It probably comes from a simple image: what is elevated, what rises. The same root appears in other Semitic languages with the same meaning. In Hebrew, we find words of the same family to express what is high or elevated. In the Greek Bible (the translation of the Old Testament into Greek called the Septuagint), this word is generally rendered by the Greek "oreos" or "oros," which means exactly the same thing.
H2022H.emploi: The word "mountain" is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible: it appears 86 times just in the provided references, and even more in reality. It is particularly dense in the historical books (Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings) where the geography of the territory of Israel is constantly expressed by the mountains that divide the land. The context changes the meaning: when we say "the mountain of Judah" or "the mountain of Ephraim," we are talking about a region; when we say "flee to the mountain" or "retreat to the mountain," we emphasize isolation and protection. As the Bible progresses, the mountain sometimes takes on a more spiritual or symbolic meaning (notably in the Psalms and the Prophets, not represented here), but in the provided historical texts, the meaning remains concrete and geographical.
H2022H.portee: For the Christian reader, the mountains of the Bible remind us how God leads His people through a rugged and difficult territory. They symbolize the obstacles to overcome and the places where one can retreat to breathe and pray. The mountains of Canaan are not an easy paradise: it is a land that requires courage to be conquered and inhabited. This teaches that the life of faith is never flat terrain, but requires climbing, progressing, and often seeking God's presence at higher altitudes.

sens: Mountain in the desert at the border of Edom where Aaron died
H2023G.detail: It is a mountain located at the edge of the land of Edom, in the desert region that the Israelites traversed after their exodus from Egypt. Moses brought Aaron and his son Eleazar there at the command of the Lord (Numbers 20:25). At the summit of this mountain, Aaron took off his priestly garments, which passed to his son Eleazar, and then Aaron died there, in the presence of the whole assembly of Israel (Numbers 20:27-28). It was a solemn moment: the entire people saw their high priest disappear before entering Canaan.
H2023G.origine: The Hebrew name Hor simply means "mountain." It is a notable peak of the red sandstone mountain range of Wadi Arabah, to the east, overlooking the caravan route. Today, it is generally identified with Jebel Harun, near the ancient city of Petra.
H2023G.emploi: Mount Hor appears ten times in the Bible, all in the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. It marks a crucial point in the desert journey: after the people left Kadesh, they arrived at Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22), where the drama of the succession of the priesthood takes place. Then, the Israelites depart to go around the land of Edom (Numbers 21:4). The mountain is also mentioned in the stages of the journey listed in chapter 33 of Numbers. It is a place of decisive events, not just a geographical landmark.
H2023G.portee: The death of Aaron at the summit of Hor reminds the reader that even the greatest servants of God face death, and that they must pass their charge to the next generation. It is also a moment of transition: Israel loses its first high priest, but the sacred function continues in Eleazar. For the Israelites in the desert, this place marked the reality of their pilgrimage — neither a return to Egypt nor an immediate entry into Canaan, but a long journey where God kept them.

sens: Mountain of Lebanon, northern boundary of the Promised Land
H2023H.detail: 1. Hor is a mountain located in the region of Lebanon, which God designates as one of the landmarks of the northern boundary of the territory that the children of Israel will conquer. In Numbers 34:7-8, this mountain marks the starting point of the northern boundary: "from the Great Sea, you shall mark out for yourselves the mountain of Hor; from the mountain of Hor, you shall turn toward Hamath."
H2023H.origine: The name "Hor" simply means "mountain" in Hebrew. It is a generic term that designates a natural geographical feature. In this biblical context, this word has become a proper noun: it identifies a specific mountain in the territory destined for Israel.
H2023H.emploi: The word Hor appears only twice in the Bible, in Numbers 34:7 and 34:8. These two occurrences are found in the passage where God outlines to Moses the exact borders of the Promised Land. Hor is mentioned exclusively as a geographical landmark, a milestone in the delineation of the northern boundary. It is never described in detail nor is it the subject of a particular narrative.
H2023H.portee: This precise mention of Hor reminds us that God clearly establishes the boundaries of the territory He promises to His people. It invites the reader to reflect on God's faithfulness to His promises and the concrete, geographically defined reality of His plan for Israel.

sens: Mountainous region of Assyria where the northern tribes of Israel were exiled
H2024.detail: 1. Hara is a region or locality located in Assyria, in the mountainous lands (the name literally means "land of mountains"). It is where King Tilgath-Pilneser deported the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh after the Assyrian conquest of the Northern Kingdom (1 Chronicles 5:26). This region, mentioned alongside Chalach, Chabor, and the river Gozan, constituted one of the destinations of the Assyrian exile of the Northern Israelites.
H2024.origine: The Hebrew name hara (הָרָא) literally means "mountain" or "land of mountains." It designates a specific geographical region in Assyria, probably in the elevated lands of northern Mesopotamia. The biblical context places Hara among the Assyrian deportation areas, alongside other regions like Gozan and Chabor.
H2024.emploi: Hara appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:26. It is mentioned in the historical account of the deportation of the Northern tribes by the Assyrian king Tilgath-Pilneser, after the fall of the kingdom of Israel. It appears in a list of destinations where the Israelite captives were established and where they remained. This mention underscores the geographical dispersion of the exiles and the definitive nature ("to this day") of this separation.

sens: Structure of stone or wood where sacrifices were offered to God
Upper part of this structure, where offerings burned
The heart or central focal point of the altar
Symbol of the meeting place between God and His people
H2025.detail:
1. The altar is the physical structure where the Israelites presented their sacrifices to God. It is a central object of worship, built according to specific dimensions and materials. In Ezekiel 43:15, the altar of the temple has detailed dimensions: "The altar was four cubits high, and four horns rose from the altar," which shows that it is indeed the complete structure of the sanctuary.
2. The word also refers to the upper part of the altar, where the offerings that burned rested. It is the "focal point" or "heart" of the altar, where the fire consumed the sacrifices offered to God, establishing a visible and tangible act of worship.
3. This term can evoke the very essence of the sacrificial act: the heart of the place where the meeting between the people and their God occurs, where sins are atoned for and communion is restored.
4. In biblical theology, the altar symbolically represents the point of contact between heaven and earth, where God accepts the offerings of His people and manifests His presence.
H2025.origine: The Hebrew word "hareel" (הַרְאֵל) combines two elements: "har" (הַר), which means "mountain" or "height," and "el" (אֵל), which means "God." Literally, "hareel" thus designates a "mountain of God" or a "focal point of God," reminding us that the altar is an elevated place, set apart, consecrated to God. This image of height reflects the spiritual significance of the altar: it is a raised place where prayers and offerings ascend to heaven.
H2025.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 43:15. It is used to describe the altar of the restored temple in Ezekiel's vision, emphasizing its monumental form with its four characteristic horns. This unique occurrence is situated in a context of very precise description of the temple's measurements, showing that "hareel" is a technical and specialized term for designating the central focal point of the altar, where the sacrificial acts of worship are accomplished.
H2025.portee: The altar reminds the believer that God has established a place and a means of meeting with His people. It is a powerful symbol of access to God, forgiveness, and communion: every sacrifice offered on the altar manifested God's willingness to accept His people and maintain the covenant. For the Christian, this altar of the Old Testament points to the ultimate sacrifice of Jesus Christ, who became the definitive "altar" on which salvation is accomplished.

sens: To take the life of someone or an animal, to put to death
To destroy, annihilate, make disappear
To cause death, to be the cause of demise
H2026.detail: 1. To kill means to take the life of a living being, human or animal, often by violence. It is the act of putting someone to death, by hand or by sword. Cain kills his brother Abel by striking him in the fields (Genesis 4:8); the Jews are commanded to kill the beast that mates with a man (Leviticus 20:15). 2. The word also designates complete destruction, the annihilation of a person or thing. God will kill the leviathan with His great sword (Isaiah 27:1), and Abimelech pays for having killed his seventy brothers (Judges 9:56). 3. In some contexts, to kill can simply mean to be the cause of death, to cause to perish. Elijah says that they seek to take his life because the children of Israel have killed the prophets (1 Kings 19:14); the Jews could defend their lives and kill those who attacked them (Esther 8:11).
H2026.origine: The Hebrew root הרג (harag) evokes the fundamental idea of striking, cutting down, taking life. It is related to the direct and violent action of destruction. The word appears about 158 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the sense of killing or causing to perish. It can be found in both passive (when one undergoes the action) and active (when one performs it) forms.
H2026.emploi: The verb to kill appears 158 times in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis to the prophets. It primarily designates murder or homicide: Cain kills Abel (Genesis 4:8), David betrays Uriah so that he may be killed in battle (2 Samuel 12:9), Abimelech kills his brothers (Judges 9:56). It is also used for judicial executions: the law commands to kill one who commits certain sins (Deuteronomy 13:9, Leviticus 20:15). The military context is frequent: one kills the enemy in battle (Joshua 8:24, Numbers 31:7). Finally, the word also applies to the destructive power of God: He will kill the sea monster (Isaiah 27:1) or devastate rebellious cities (Judges 9:45).
H2026.portee: This word reveals the gravity of murder in the eyes of God. To kill an innocent person is to shed blood without right, which cries out for vengeance before the Lord. At the same time, God reserves the right to give and take life, and He delegates to authorities the power to judge and punish crimes. For the believer, this word reminds us of the sacredness of human life, created in the image of God, and the call to justice and mercy.

sens: Action of killing en masse, causing a large number of deaths
Massacre, carnage
Murder, homicide
H2027.detail:
1. The word describes the action of killing, taking someone's life by violence. It is a deliberate act, often massive and brutal. In Esther 9:5, the Jews "killed" their enemies with the sword: this is the action verb that designates the murderous act itself.

2. When several people are killed together, it is referred to as carnage or massacre — a bloody event of great magnitude. Isaiah 30:25 mentions "the day of great carnage," an apocalyptic image of massive destruction; Ezekiel 26:15 describes the "carnage" in Tyre, the ruined city.

3. The word can also mean slaughtering, that is, the violent and often ritual killing. Proverbs 24:11 speaks of those "who are to be slaughtered" — an image of victims led to death like animals.
H2027.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of striking, of delivering blows. It is related to verbs that mean "to kill" or "to strike fatally." The literal meaning is therefore: to deliver blows that kill, to strike until death. It is a concrete word, forged on the brutal realism of violence.
H2027.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel) and in the account of Esther. It designates either the act of killing (Esther 9:5), or the state of massive slaughter (Isaiah 30:25; Ezekiel 26:15), or the threat of death (Proverbs 24:11). The context varies: it can describe a just vengeance (Esther), an apocalyptic divine judgment (Isaiah), the ruin of a city (Ezekiel), or a call to save the innocent (Proverbs). It is always serious and violent language.
H2027.portee: This word reminds the reader of the real and terrible nature of human violence and divine judgment. It invites the reader to take seriously the warning against death — whether it is unjustly suffered (Proverbs 24:11: rescuing the innocent) or inflicted by God (Isaiah, Ezekiel: the terrible judgments of the Lord). It is a vocabulary that does not sugarcoat reality, but challenges the conscience.

sens: To massacre, to kill en masse
The bloody destruction of a multitude of people
Prophetic image of divine judgment
H2028G.detail:
1. This Hebrew word designates the act of killing, murder, or execution. It is the concrete action of shedding blood, destroying one or more lives by violence.

2. Used in the plural or collectively, it evokes carnage, that is, mass death, the horrible spectacle of many bodies killed together. Jeremiah speaks of "the valley of carnage" (Jeremiah 7:32) to designate what will become a battlefield or a mass grave.

3. In both usages here, this word takes on prophetic force: God renames Topheth (the traditional place of idol worship) "valley of carnage" to announce that this place will become the theater of massive death, divine punishment against the idolatry of the people. It is the image of a terrible and inevitable judgment.
H2028G.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to strike," "to kill." Its basic image is that of violent death, the blow that takes life. In Hebrew, several words from the same family express murder, homicide, or violent death. The word appears infrequently in the Old Testament, which underscores its dramatic weight: it is reserved for moments when mass death is at the heart of the prophetic message.
H2028G.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the prophet Jeremiah. In Jeremiah 7:32 and 19:6, it serves the same prophetic oracle: God announces that he will rename the valley of Ben-Hinnom (Topheth) as "valley of carnage." This valley was the site of idol worship and human sacrifices; by renaming it, God promises that it will become a massive cemetery where the dead of Jerusalem will be buried due to lack of space. The context is one of divine judgment on the persistent sin of the people.
H2028G.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the refusal to repent leads to terrible and real consequences. Topheth, a place of rebellion against God, becomes a place of mass death: it is a solemn warning. The prophecy invites us to take seriously the gravity of sin and the reality of divine judgment, while not ignoring that this threat aims to call the people to conversion.

sens: Action of killing, slaughtering animals
To massacre, to exterminate en masse
Violent and inevitable destruction
H2028H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of killing and slaughtering animals intended for consumption or sacrifice. In Zechariah 11:4 and 11:7, it literally refers to sheep "destined for slaughter," that is, marked for death — they are already marked for death, without hope of salvation.
2. The word is used figuratively to describe a massacre, an extermination en masse. In Jeremiah 12:3, the prophet pleads with the Lord to "remove" the wicked "like sheep to be slaughtered" and to prepare them "for the day of carnage," that is, to deliver them to total destruction: he evokes the image of the flock being led to the slaughterhouse to express an inevitable and widespread ruin.
H2028H.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to kill, to strike, to slaughter." It is a feminine noun that describes the action itself — the slaughter — rather than the one who kills. The basic image is that of ritual or food slaughter: the fatal blow, the blood shed, the certain end. The word appears rarely in the Bible, always to evoke a programmed, inevitable death.
H2028H.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Old Testament, all in the 6th-century prophets (Jeremiah and Zechariah). It always describes sheep destined for slaughter (Zechariah 11:4, 11:7) or, figuratively, the destruction of the wicked (Jeremiah 12:3). The image of sheep being led to the slaughter, defenseless and without recourse, becomes, in Jeremiah, the metaphor for the helplessness of God's enemies in the face of his inevitable judgment. The context is always that of divine judgment or a sealed fate.
H2028H.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the harshness of divine judgment: one who rebels against God is like an animal destined for slaughter, with no way out. But it also invites us to see in this image the vulnerability of the defenseless — the miserable sheep of Zechariah 11:7 — and the responsibility of the one who keeps them. It is a call to fear God and to show compassion towards the weak.

sens: To become pregnant, to carry a child in the womb
To have an idea, a project; to form a design
To engender, to give birth
H2029.detail:
1. To become pregnant, to carry a child: this is the most common physical meaning. Rebecca "became pregnant" after Isaac prayed for her (Genesis 25:21), and Hannah "became pregnant" after the Lord visited her (1 Samuel 2:21). The word designates the moment when a woman begins to carry the child.
2. To form a project, a design, particularly an evil design: the psalmist says of the wicked that he "conceives iniquity" (Psalms 7:15), meaning that he forms a wicked plan in his heart, just as one forms a child. Similarly, Isaiah speaks of those who "conceive iniquity" (Isaiah 59:4).
3. To give birth: this is the culmination of conception. Eve "conceived and bore Cain" (Genesis 4:1). The word can also be used figuratively: evil designs "bring forth emptiness" (Psalms 7:15).
H2029.origine: The Hebrew root ha.rah fundamentally evokes the idea of making fruitful, of causing to bear fruit. It is related to the notion of begetting and fertility. The word is used in various grammatical forms (simple, passive, intensive) to designate both physical conception and, by extension, the formation of an idea or project in the mind. This extension from physical meaning to moral meaning is natural: just as a woman carries a child, one also carries a project or intention in one's heart.
H2029.emploi: The verb appears 42 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis and historical narratives. It is frequently used to recount the conceptions of the patriarchal women: Eve, Rebecca, Rachel, Bilhah, Hannah, Bathsheba. It is also found in the Psalms and the prophets to describe the moral conception of evil: the wicked conceives iniquity (Psalms 7:15, Isaiah 59:4, Isaiah 59:13), and the text plays on the image of childbirth to show that these projects result in empty or destructive fruits. The verb is also used figuratively for the acts of God or His word that brings forth a people or new realities.
H2029.portee: This word reminds the reader that motherhood and fertility are a gift from God, not a natural acquisition. It also shows that our thoughts, our projects, our moral intentions are as important in God's eyes as our actions: we "conceive" evil before we do it. The parallel between physical childbirth and the birthing of sin invites vigilance over our secret thoughts, which germinate like new life and need to be judged in the light of God.

sens: The state of a woman carrying a child in her womb
A woman about to give birth
A situation characterized by carrying an unborn child
H2030A.detail:
1. A woman is pregnant when she carries a child in her womb, from the moment of conception until childbirth. This is the natural state of awaiting motherhood. The angel tells Hagar: "You are pregnant, and you will bear a son" (Genesis 16:11), announcing both her pregnancy and her impending deliverance.
2. The word also designates a woman who is at the end of her pregnancy and close to giving birth. Phinehas's wife was "pregnant and about to give birth" (1 Samuel 4:19) when she received the bad news that caused her to go into labor.
3. The word is used to speak of the condition of one who carries an unborn child: it is a situation of transformation of the body and anticipation. When the prophet Elisha denounces the cruelties of King Hazael, he mentions that he will "rip open the bellies of their pregnant women" (2 Kings 8:12), highlighting the atrocity of the crime against life itself.
H2030A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be heavy" or "to be filled." The pregnant woman indeed carries a weight that fills her body. This simple and concrete image of weight and fullness has attached itself to the word to specifically designate pregnancy. Hebrew also uses a related form, harir yah (הָרִיָּה), with a slight grammatical variation but the same meaning.
H2030A.emploi: The word appears about fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in genealogical and covenant narratives (Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel), in laws (Exodus), and among the prophets who announce or judge (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos). It is first encountered when God announces a promised birth: to Hagar (Genesis 16:11), to Samson's mother (Judges 13:5), to Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:5), and to the young girl in Isaiah 7:14. The word is also used in tragic contexts where pregnancy becomes a threat: pregnant women are victims of violence (2 Kings 8:12; Amos 1:13). It also appears in a shameful situation when Tamar must prove that she carries Judah's child (Genesis 38:25). Thus, the word oscillates between the announcement of grace and the evocation of suffering.
H2030A.portee: This word reminds us that life is transmitted and that motherhood is at the heart of God's design: the greatest promises pass through a pregnant woman (Emmanuel in Isaiah 7:14). But it also reveals the fragility of the weak: the pregnant woman becomes a symbol of vulnerability, and her protection is a sign of justice. Recognizing the sacredness of the growing life is to honor God who placed it there.

sens: Who carries a child in her womb, who is in a state of pregnancy
H2030B.detail: 1. Who carries a child in her womb, who is in a state of pregnancy — this is the natural state of a woman awaiting a child. The text of Hosea 13:16 uses it in a terrible context: the punishment of Samaria will be so brutal that even pregnant women will be killed, showing the extreme violence of divine judgment.
H2030B.origine: This Hebrew word is a variant of a more common word (הָרָה, ha.rah) that means exactly the same thing. Both spellings appear in biblical Hebrew without a difference in meaning. The root expresses the idea of being heavy, burdened — which corresponds well to the physical image of pregnancy.
H2030B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 13:16, in a judgment oracle against Samaria. It specifically designates women who carry a child, to emphasize that the punishment will be total and terrible, sparing no one — not even those who are in the vulnerability of pregnancy. This context is one of prophetic threat.
H2030B.portee: This word reminds us that Scripture does not hide the harsh realities of divine judgment and sin. It also invites us to see pregnancy as a condition of human vulnerability — one that God protects and values elsewhere in the Bible.
