The contrast between this destructive image and the love that God shows for life helps the reader to measure the gravity of rebellion against God.

sens: Thought that constantly returns to the mind
Image or vision that haunts the imagination
Concern that occupies the soul
H2031.detail:
1. The word designates a thought that constantly returns, an idea that imposes itself on the mind against one's will. In Daniel 4:5, King Nebuchadnezzar speaks of the thoughts of which he is "pursued" on his bed: these are the images of the dream that haunt him, tormenting him without his ability to free himself from them.
2. It is also the mental image itself, the representation one has of something, often involuntarily. The vision of the royal dream constantly returns to Nebuchadnezzar, occupying him entirely.
3. More broadly, it is the concern that seizes the soul and fills it with anxiety, like an obsession. The context of Daniel shows how this mental pursuit generates fear and dread.
H2031.origine: The Hebrew word harhor comes from a root that expresses the idea of turning around, of returning constantly. This image of what "turns" in the mind captures well the repetitive and haunting nature of a thought that does not leave us. It is a noun formed from a verbal root, emphasizing the incessant movement of the imagination.
H2031.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:5. The context is that of the prophetic dream that torments King Nebuchadnezzar: the dream images constantly return to his mind, pursuing him even on his bed, filling him with dread. The singular usage shows the intensity of the phenomenon — it is not a mere passing thought, but a mental obsession.
H2031.portee: This word reminds us that the images and thoughts that seize our minds carry weight and can deeply disturb us. In Nebuchadnezzar's case, the mental pursuit of the dream becomes the starting point of an encounter with God. This suggests that our concerns and inner torments, far from being insignificant, can be the means by which God speaks to us and calls us to transformation.

sens: State of a pregnant woman, from the moment she conceives until childbirth
Ability to conceive, to become pregnant
Act of conceiving a child
H2032.detail:
1. Pregnancy is the physiological state of a woman carrying a child in her womb after conception. In Genesis 3:16, God speaks to Eve about the pains associated with pregnancies, showing that this state is accompanied by pain and labor — an echo of the consequences of sin on the human body.
2. The word also designates the very act of conceiving, of becoming pregnant: Ruth 4:13 recounts that "the Lord allowed Ruth to conceive," meaning He granted her to become pregnant and bear a son.
3. More broadly, it evokes fertility itself, the blessing of having children. In Hosea 9:11, the loss of pregnancy symbolizes divine abandonment and misfortune: Ephraim will lose all descendants, which was an existential drama in biblical antiquity.
H2032.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to conceive" or "to bear." It is formed on the nominal model of concrete terms, anchoring the meaning in bodily reality. The same family of words expresses the act of conceiving, becoming pregnant, and the resulting state — pregnancy. It is a simple and direct term, without detour.
H2032.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, always in contexts that emphasize the importance of fertility. In Genesis 3:16, it is linked to human suffering following original sin. In Ruth 4:13, it expresses divine intervention granting offspring — a blessing after barrenness. In Hosea 9:11, it signifies the absence of descendants as divine punishment. The word thus carries spiritual value: pregnancy is never neutral in the Bible; it manifests either the blessing of God, the fruit of sin, or the absence of His favor.
H2032.portee: This word reminds the reader that motherhood and fertility occupy a central place in the biblical vision of human life. It is not just a biological process, but a reality marked by divine Providence, suffering, and hope. For a believing woman, pregnancy becomes an opportunity to recognize God's work in her body and to reflect on her relationship with Him.

sens: Warrior of David's guard
H2033.detail: Haror is the title given to Shammoth, one of the elite warriors who formed the guard of King David. This title seems to indicate his origin or belonging to a particular group among the bravest soldiers of the kingdom.
H2033.origine: The word Haror is a spelling variant related to Harod (a famous water source in Israel, also mentioned in 1 Samuel 29:1). This title suggests a mountain origin or a specific geographical provenance, a characteristic by which the names of David's warriors were marked to identify them.
H2033.emploi: Haror appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:27, where it qualifies Shammoth, one of the thirty warriors chosen by David. These lists of elite warriors enumerated the most faithful and valiant men of the king, and the title or epithet attached to each name allowed them to be distinguished by their origin or qualities.

sens: State of destruction of a dwelling or construction
Remains of a destroyed or dilapidated building
Figuratively: collapse, decline of an institution or lineage
H2034.detail:
1. Ruin is primarily the state of what has collapsed, been destroyed, or annihilated. It is the result of complete destruction. The word evokes the debris of a building or a city reduced to nothing.
2. It also refers to the visible remains, the vestiges of a once beautiful or significant construction. In Amos 9:11, God speaks of raising up and rebuilding "the ruins" of the house of David: there are breaches, cracks, but something remains to be restored.
3. In a figurative and theological sense, it is the collapse of a lineage, a dynasty, or a divine project that seemed abandoned. When God says, "I will raise up its ruin," He promises to restore what appears to be lost forever.
H2034.origine: The Hebrew word הֲרִיסָה (harisah) comes from the Hebrew root רסס (hARAC), which means "to demolish," "to bring down," "to destroy." It is a feminine noun that designates the state or action of reducing to ruin. The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to destruction. The underlying verb evokes the idea of breaking, shattering what is standing.
H2034.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Amos 9:11, in a major messianic prophecy. God promises to raise up "the ruins" of the house of David, in other words, to restore a dynasty and a nation that seem irreparably lost. The context is that of judgment: Israel has been punished, scattered, but the divine promise remains. The word is used to express total desolation but also, and this is crucial, the possibility and certainty of restoration.
H2034.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Church and the people of God, even reduced to the appearance of nothingness, are never beyond divine restoration. Like the ruins of the house of David, what seems destroyed can be raised up by the power of God. It is a word of hope in Jesus Christ, heir and restorer of the promise made to David.

sens: complete destruction of a city or building
state of desolation and abandonment that results
collapse, annihilation
H2035.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical destruction of a city or its buildings — what remains are debris and rubble. In Isaiah 49:19, God promises Jerusalem that its "devastated places," once in ruins, will soon be repopulated: this is the image of a city annihilated, then rebuilt.
2. More broadly, it evokes the state of desolation that follows destruction — abandonment, silence, absence of life. It is not only the destroyed stones, but also the misfortune and suffering that have struck the people.
3. In a figurative sense, it can denote any moral or spiritual annihilation — the ruin of a person, a family, an entire nation. It is the biblical image of what falls and does not rise again, except by the grace of God.
H2035.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root הרס (haras), which means "to destroy, to tear down, to demolish." It evokes the violent action of overturning or bringing down what was standing. The form used here is an abstract feminine noun that emphasizes the state or process of destruction rather than a simple destroyed object.
H2035.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 49:19. It is used in a context of prophetic consolation: the prophet announces to the exiled people that their destroyed cities will be restored and repopulated, that ruin will give way to prosperity. It is a rare but expressive word, chosen to highlight the extent of the transformation that God will bring about.
H2035.portee: This verse speaks to the heart of those who know disaster, loss, or collapse. It reminds us that even the most complete ruins are not permanent in God's eyes — today's destruction can become the starting point for restoration. It is a promise of uplift for those who trust in Him.

sens: Canaanite king of Gezer at the time of Israel's conquest
H2036.detail: Horam is a Canaanite king who reigns over the city of Gezer during the conquest of the land by Joshua. Learning that the city of Lachish is besieged by the Israelites, he marches to its rescue with his army. Joshua completely defeats him: the king and all his people are struck down without any escape (Joshua 10:33).
H2036.origine: The name Horam means "exalted" in Hebrew, reflecting the high status of a king. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, during Joshua's early military campaigns in the Promised Land. His brief appearance symbolizes the resistance of Canaanite kings against the Israelite advance.
H2036.emploi: Horam appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 10:33. He is featured in the account of the conquest wars led by Joshua against the Canaanite cities. His swift intervention to defend Lachish shows that the Canaanite kings were aware of the threat posed by Joshua's army and attempted to assist one another. His total defeat and that of his people illustrate the irresistible power of the conquest and the fulfillment of God's promise to Israel.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H2037.detail: Harum is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:8. He is the son of Kots and the brother of Anub and Zobebah. His name means "exalted." He is best known as the father of Aharhel, whose descendants are listed in this genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
H2037.origine: The name Harum comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be elevated, exalted." It belongs to the family of names that express a prominent or honorable position. This name reflects an Old Testament theology where exaltation is often linked to divine favor.
H2037.emploi: Harum appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:8. He is listed in the genealogy of Judah, a record of the descendants of the tribes of Israel established after the exile. His only known role is being the father of Aharhel, suggesting that there was a notable lineage associated with his name in the genealogies of the tribe.

sens: fortified place in Israel mentioned in the words of the prophet Amos
H2038.detail: Harmon is a place that the prophet Amos mentions in his prophecy against Israel. Its name means "high fortress," suggesting a strategic location, perhaps a fortified height. The context in which Amos mentions it speaks of divine judgments that will come upon the people of Israel who have forgotten God.
H2038.origine: The name Harmon comes from a root meaning "high" or "elevated," hence the image of a fortress built on a dominant position. Its meaning evokes a place of refuge or defense. The exact location has not been formally identified by archaeologists, although specialists have proposed several locations in the West Bank or Transjordan.
H2038.emploi: Harmon appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 4:3. Amos uses it to declare a prophetic judgment: he announces that the inhabitants of Israel will be driven "toward the mountain of Harmon." This passage is part of a series of warnings addressed to the women of Samaria who oppress the poor and have refused to return to God despite His repeated calls.

sens: son of Terah, brother of Abraham
father of Lot, Milcah, and Iscah
city in Mesopotamia where the descendants of Nahor settled
H2039G.detail:
1. Haran is the youngest son of Terah and the brother of Abraham and Nahor. He is born and dies in Ur of the Chaldeans, before leaving this city with his family (Genesis 11:26-28). His name means "mountaineer" in Hebrew.
2. Haran is the father of three children: Lot, Milcah, and Iscah. Lot will become Abraham's traveling companion and play an important role in the patriarchal narrative (Genesis 11:27, 11:29).
3. Haran also refers to a city in Mesopotamia, probably located in the fertile region between the Khabur and the Euphrates, at the foot of Mount Masius. Abraham and his family stop there during their migration to Canaan (Genesis 11:31), and the descendants of Nahor, Abraham's brother, settle there.
H2039G.origine: The name Haran comes from a Hebrew root evoking the mountain or altitude. The place bearing this name is a mountainous area of high Mesopotamia, a historical region known to be the cradle of Semitic peoples.
H2039G.emploi: Haran appears five times in Genesis, primarily in chapter 11. He is first presented as the third son of Terah, who died in Ur before the family's departure to Canaan. His genealogical importance is crucial: he is the father of Lot, who accompanies Abraham and becomes a key figure in the patriarchal narrative. The text also mentions that his daughters Milcah and Iscah will make significant marriages. The city of Haran, where the family stops, will become an important center of Abraham's genealogy, as it is where the descendants of Nahor settle.
H2039G.portee: Haran reminds us that even Abraham's close relatives, though called by God to enter into His covenant, do not all follow the same path. His death before the great migration underscores the biblical theme of departure and the rupture that faith demands. His children, particularly Lot, embody the consequences and complications of this family legacy in the history of salvation.

sens: A Levite of the tribe of Gershon
son of Shimei and brother of Shelomith
H2039H.detail: Haran is a Levite belonging to the family of Gershon, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Shimei and the brother of Shelomith and Haziel. At the time of King David, these three brothers are listed as heads of paternal houses in the family of Laadan, responsible for organizing the Levites of the temple (1 Chronicles 23:9).
H2039H.origine: The name Haran means "mountaineer" or "one of the mountains." In the Hebrew Old Testament, it also designates a region and other people, but this entry concerns only the Levite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 23:9, son of Shimei.
H2039H.emploi: Haran appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 23:9. He is cited in the list of the descendants of Levi established by King David to organize the temple service. With his brothers Shelomith and Haziel, he was part of the heads of the Levitical families and played a role in the religious administration of Israel during David's time.

sens: To throw down, demolish a structure
To break, shatter an object
To destroy a kingdom, a power
To morally bring down, ruin someone
H2040.detail:
1. Overthrow literally means to throw down a structure: to demolish a wall, an altar, a house. For example, in Exodus 23:24, the people must overthrow the altars of false gods. It is a violent and complete act: what is overthrown no longer stands.

2. The word also describes the act of breaking or shattering an object or a part of the body. In Psalms 58:7, we ask God to break the teeth of the wicked in their mouths: a targeted and definitive destruction.

3. Overthrow is used to describe the fall of a kingdom or political power. In Jeremiah 50:15, the walls of Babylon are overthrown, its foundations collapse: it is the downfall of an empire. Only God has the power to overthrow nations.

4. The word can also mean to ruin someone morally or spiritually, to bring them low from their power. In Isaiah 22:19, God says to Shebna: "I will thrust you from your office" — literally, to overthrow you from your position. It is to lose all credit and authority.
H2040.origine: The Hebrew verb hāraś denotes the action of breaking, shattering, throwing down. Its basic image is that of a violent gesture that destroys a structure. The root evokes rupture, radical destruction. In Hebrew, there are related words that share this idea of destruction — to overthrow, to break, to demolish. It is a very ancient word, common in contexts of war and divine judgment.
H2040.emploi: This verb appears 42 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is particularly frequent in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah), where it describes God's judgments against nations and idols. It is also found in Psalms and Proverbs. The word applies to human acts (overthrowing an altar, a wall) and to God's action (who overthrows kingdoms). Its meaning varies little: it always expresses violent and definitive destruction, often irreversible. It is a strong term that marks the totality of ruin.
H2040.portee: Overthrow reminds us that only God controls history and that no human power, no empire can resist His will. The word invites us to turn our worship away from false gods and the powers of the world, which can be overthrown. For the believer, it is a source of assurance: whoever places their trust in God will not be overthrown, while every structure built away from God will eventually collapse.

sens: Overthrow or complete ruin of a city or a people
In Isaiah's vision, one of the symbolic names given to a city in Egypt during its judgment
H2041.detail:
1. The word denotes the act of destroying, of overturning something completely — particularly a city or a structure. It is total ruin, annihilation. In Isaiah 19:18, an Egyptian city receives the name "destruction" as a sign of God's judgment on Egypt.

2. In Isaiah's prophecy, this term becomes a symbolic name: it denotes the future transformation of an Egyptian city, which will recognize the Lord and speak the language of Canaan. The name "destruction" expresses both the past or imminent judgment and the spiritual transformation of that place.
H2041.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of breaking, demolishing. It is linked to the concrete image of overthrowing or collapsing. In the Hebrew Bible, this word carries a theological dimension: destruction is often the result of divine judgment on injustice and idolatry.
H2041.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond, in Isaiah 19:18. The Bible reports a prophecy concerning Egypt: in a future time, five cities in the land will speak the language of Canaan and swear by the Lord. One of them will be named "city of destruction" — probably an ancient temple or sanctuary in Egypt (On-Heliopolis according to the commentaries). This name emphasizes the divine judgment that transforms places of false worship into witnesses of the true God.
H2041.portee: This prophecy reminds us that God spares no nation, and that even foreign and idolatrous powers will know His judgment. It also announces a restoration: destruction is not an end, but the prelude to the recognition of the true God. For the believer, this encourages trust in the Lord's judgment, which breaks false gods and leads His enemies to recognize Him.

sens: Elevated geographical relief, mountain range
Place of strength and stability
Symbol of grandeur and divine majesty
Territory or possession
Image of God's justice and power
H2042.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a geographical relief: a mountain or a mountain range. This is the concrete geographical sense of the term, as when it speaks of the "mountains of the East" from which Balaam came (Numbers 23:7), or the "everlasting hills" of the land of Israel (Deuteronomy 33:15).
2. Mountains represent a place of solidity and permanence: something stable and unchanging. When Psalm 36:7 compares divine justice to the "mountains of God," it evokes this unshakeable stability — justice is as solid as a mountain.
3. The mountain becomes an image of majesty and power. Psalm 76:5 states that the Lord is "more majestic" than the "mountains of robbers," placing God above all, even the most imposing forces.
4. A mountain can denote a territory or possession: when Jeremiah speaks of "my mountain," he refers to the land of Israel itself, considered as the property of the people (Jeremiah 17:3).
5. Poetically, the mountain symbolizes the stable cosmic order that God maintains. This is why it appears in images of blessing and eternity (Psalm 133:3).
H2042.origine: The Hebrew word הָרָר (harar) is a variant of the more common word הַר (har), "mountain." It is an alternative form, perhaps older or regional, of the same root word. The root evokes the idea of "to rise" or "to dominate." The word belongs to the fundamental vocabulary of biblical geography: mountains play a major role in the Old Testament, both as geographical landmarks and as theological symbols.
H2042.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mostly in biblical poetry (Psalms, Song of Solomon, Jeremiah, Habakkuk). It is almost always used in the sense of a mountain range or elevated relief. In historical and narrative passages (Numbers, Deuteronomy), it refers to real mountains: those of the East (Numbers 23:7) or those of the land of Israel (Deuteronomy 33:15). In poetry, particularly in the Psalms, it takes on a symbolic charge: mountains become metaphors for divine strength, justice, majesty, or cosmic stability. The context determines whether the word remains concrete or becomes a spiritual image.
H2042.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God is greater and more stable than any earthly obstacle. Mountains, despite their seemingly unshakeable appearance, are nothing compared to divine power and justice. It is also an invitation to meditate on the solidity of God's promise: as the mountains endure, so the blessing of the Lord is eternal.

sens: inhabitant ou descendant de Harar ou de Harod
guerrier de David issu de cette région
H2043.detail:
1. Hararite designates someone from or descended from Harar (or perhaps Harod), a mountainous region. The name evokes a "mountain dweller." It is first encountered in 2 Samuel 23:11, where it qualifies Shammah, one of David's mighty warriors.
2. This term applies to several of David's most renowned men: Shammah, Agai, and Ahijah are all presented as Hararites, meaning elite soldiers from this mountainous region. Their presence in the list of warriors (2 Samuel 23) shows that being a Hararite was a mark of distinction.
H2043.origine: The word Hararite comes from the place name Harar (or perhaps Harod), a mountainous area. The Hebrew root הַר (har) means "mountain." Hararite is thus a demonym (a name that indicates geographical origin), formed to indicate belonging to this region. This type of designation was common: warriors were identified by their place of origin, which informed about their physical strength and reputation.
H2043.emploi: The word Hararite appears four times in Scripture, exclusively in the lists of David's warriors (2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11). It qualifies at least three renowned warriors: Shammah (2 Samuel 23:11), Agai, and Ahijah (2 Samuel 23:33; 1 Chronicles 11:34-35). These men are among David's "mighty men," suggesting that Harar was known for producing formidable soldiers. The fact that several of these fighters are specifically identified as Hararites indicates that their origin was worthy of mention.
H2043.portee: These Hararites remind us that God equipped David with warriors from all regions of Israel, each bringing their strength and experience. Their names recorded in Scripture show that God honors faithful service, regardless of geographical origin. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that the strength of God's service comes from those who are faithful, wherever they come from.

sens: Homme de l'époque de la Monarchie unie israélite
Père de guerriers au service du roi David
H2044.detail:
1. Bené-Haschem is a man's name mentioned in the lists of warriors from the time of King David. He is encountered in 1 Chronicles 11:34 among the king's mighty men, making him a historical figure from the time when David ruled over united Israel.
2. He is known as the father of warriors who served alongside David. His son Jonathan is among these elite men. The name "Bené-Haschem" literally means "the sons of Haschem" (bené = sons, in Hebrew), indicating that the father is designated by reference to his warrior descendants.
H2044.origine: The name Haschem comes from the Hebrew "shem" which evokes something fat or corpulent. It is a simple patronymic attested in 2 Samuel 23:32 in the form Jashen, and in 1 Chronicles 11:34 in the form Haschem. These two names refer to the same character. Patronymics of this kind, formed based on physical traits or characteristics, are common in ancient Israel.
H2044.emploi: Bené-Haschem appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:34. He is listed among the Thirty, David's elite warriors. This list revises and complements that of 2 Samuel 23, where the same character is called Jashen. The use of the patronymic "Bené-Haschem" (the sons of Haschem) allows for the identification of the father through his children, notably Jonathan, who is distinguished by his bravery alongside David.

sens: Action de faire entendre, de porter une nouvelle à quelqu'un
Message ou nouvelle rapportée
Communication, information transmise oralement
H2045.detail: 1. The word designates the action of conveying news to someone, bringing it to their ears. In Ezekiel 24:26, a fugitive comes to "announce" to Ezekiel the fall of Jerusalem: it is about orally communicating an important event. 2. It is the news itself, what is heard and reported — the information transmitted from one person to another. 3. More broadly, it encompasses any act of communication by word, any transmission of a message.
H2045.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root שׁמע (shama), which means "to hear." It evokes the action of listening, receiving through the ear. The formative suffix creates a noun of action: it is thus "the act of hearing" or "what is heard." This family of words is very present in the Old Testament to speak of listening and receiving the word.
H2045.emploi: This word appears only once in Ezekiel 24:26, in the context of the siege of Jerusalem. The prophet announces that the destruction of the city will be so complete that fugitives will bring the news to those who remain. The usage emphasizes the importance of direct and personal communication: it is face to face, from mouth to ear, that serious news is transmitted in the Bible.
H2045.portee: This word reminds us of the power of orally transmitted words in the life of Israel. For the Christian, it evokes the importance of communicating important messages — especially the Word of God — in a direct and lively manner. It is through oral announcement that faith spreads and people are reached.

sens: Eunuch in the service of Queen Esther in the palace of King Ahasuerus
H2047.detail: Hathac is an eunuch, meaning a castrated servant assigned delicate missions in the Persian royal palace. He appears only in the book of Esther, where he plays a role as a trusted messenger between Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai. When Mordecai learns of a plot against the Jews, Esther tasks him with going to ask what is happening (Esther 4:5). Hathac then becomes the intermediary: he finds Mordecai in the city square (Esther 4:6), brings Esther his words of warning (Esther 4:9), and then conveys to Mordecai the queen's instructions (Esther 4:10). His role, although brief, is crucial as it allows Esther and Mordecai to consult and implement the plan that will save the Jewish people.
H2047.origine: The name Hathac means "truly" or "really" in Hebrew. Although he is a Persian employed in the palace of Ahasuerus, his name carries a Semitic meaning, which is not surprising in the context of the book of Esther where Jews and Persians coexist. As a royal eunuch, Hathac belongs to a category of servants common in ancient Eastern courts.
H2047.emploi: Hathac appears only in the book of Esther, in chapters 4, verses 5, 6, 9, and 10. He is a minor but functional character in the narrative of Jewish deliverance. Esther uses him exclusively as a trusted messenger to communicate with Mordecai without King Ahasuerus knowing. Each use of the name shows Hathac fulfilling a task: responding to Esther's call, going to Mordecai, reporting his words, and then relaying the queen's orders. His discretion and reliability make him an indispensable intermediary for the happy resolution of the story.

sens: to ridicule someone in words, with derision and contempt
to make fun of someone's beliefs or powers
H2048A.detail:
1. To mock means to address someone with scornful and contemptuous words to ridicule them. Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal by suggesting that their god is sleeping or busy elsewhere, highlighting the absurdity of their ineffective prayers (1 Kings 18:27).
2. The word also carries the idea of making fun of, questioning the powers or abilities of the one being mocked. Elijah thus casts doubt on the power of Baal by offering ironic and disdainful explanations for his silence.
H2048A.origine: The Hebrew verb הָתַל (hatal) belongs to a root that expresses the idea of playing with someone, treating them lightly and with contempt. The form used here (Piel) intensifies this meaning: not just to mock, but truly to mock, to ridicule insistently. This verb is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible.
H2048A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 1 Kings 18:27, in the scene where Elijah confronts the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. After allowing the prophets of Baal to pray in vain for hours, Elijah publicly mocks them in a scathing manner. This mockery is an act of religious defiance: Elijah highlights Baal's impotence in the face of the God of Israel. The mockery here serves as a tool for spiritual pedagogy and prophetic challenge.
H2048A.portee: This word shows us how a prophet of God can use irony and mockery, not out of personal cruelty, but to expose religious error and weaken trust in a false deity. For the reader, Elijah becomes a model of prophetic courage: he is not afraid to publicly ridicule those who mislead the people, because the truth of the living God takes precedence. The scene reminds us that true faith does not fear confrontation with idolatry.

sens: to mock someone by lying to them or deceiving them
to take advantage of someone's gullibility by hiding the truth
to mystify, to intentionally mislead
H2048B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to mock someone by telling them lies to make fun of them. Jacob accuses Laban: "Your father has played me, and has changed my wages ten times" (Genesis 31:7) — he says this in anger, as Laban has deceived him in the marriage contract. Samson plays with Delilah several times by giving her false explanations about his strength: "You have played me, you have told me lies" (Judges 16:10). This is a deception that ridicules the victim.
2. The word also refers to the abuse of trust: taking advantage of someone's naivety or love to deceive them. Delilah says to Samson: "How can you say: I love you! since you have played me?" (Judges 16:15) — she feels betrayed. Pharaoh wants to deceive Moses by promising the departure of the people without fulfilling it (Exodus 8:25).
3. Broadly speaking, it means to intentionally mislead someone, to mystify them. Job asks: "Or will you deceive him as one deceives a man?" (Job 13:9) — he speaks of someone who deceives themselves by feigning righteousness.
H2048B.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּלַל (talal) comes from a root expressing the idea of mocking or playing with someone (Hebrew לוּל, lul). In biblical Hebrew, the family of this word always denotes an action of intentional deception or derision. The context of its uses shows that it is a voluntary act, never an accident: one deceives because one wants to deceive.
H2048B.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in accounts of personal deception. In the story of Jacob and Laban (Genesis 31:7), it describes the abuse of managerial authority. In the story of Samson and Delilah (Judges 16:10, 13, 15), it appears three times to show the systematic repetition of romantic deception. With Pharaoh (Exodus 8:25), it is political cunning. In Job (13:9), it is religious deception, that of one who presents false piety. The word never speaks of accidental deception: it is always conscious, often cruel.
H2048B.portee: This word reminds us that deception is a serious sin in the eyes of God. It hurts the one who endures it and offers God a heart that does not love the truth. The believer learns that one cannot build a relationship—marriage, friendship, trust—on lies: Samson pays the price, as does Laban. It is a call to sincerity and honesty in all human relationships.

sens: one who mocks, who ridicules
an attitude of derision towards someone or something
H2049.detail:
1. The mocker is one who openly mocks, who ridicules with hurtful words. In Job 17:2, Job feels surrounded by mockers who belittle him with their insults — these are people who do not respect his suffering and ridicule him.
2. The word also designates the attitude itself: this mockery, this derision that refuses to take seriously the distress of a person. It is a form of contempt expressed through words or looks.
H2049.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root תול (tôl), which means "to deceive, seduce, mislead." Mockery is a word that deceives and seeks to bring the other down — it diverts the truth to ridicule. This verb also appears in other forms in Hebrew to denote deception or misleading.
H2049.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 17:2. Job is going through a terrible trial — he is sick, ruined, plagued by doubt — and his friends, instead of comforting him, mock him. They become his mockers, those who add insult to injury. This context shows that mockery is particularly cruel when it strikes one who is already suffering.
H2049.portee: This word from Job reminds us of the destructive power of mockery: it wounds the heart, isolates the one who suffers, and adds pain to pain. For the Christian, it invites us to flee from gossip and ridicule, and to instead welcome those who suffer with compassion and respect.

sens: To throw oneself against someone with force and the intention of causing harm
To assault, to overwhelm someone with blows or attacks
To conspire against someone, to prepare their ruin
H2050.detail:
1. The word describes the action of violently rushing against someone, like a crowd that throws itself upon prey. It is a physical and brutal assault: in Psalm 62:4, the psalmist's enemies all throw themselves upon him to bring him down, crushing him like one topples a shaky wall.
2. It also conveys the idea of overwhelming someone, crushing them under the weight of repeated attacks. The one who is the object of the verb finds themselves submerged, overwhelmed by the violence or malice of their adversaries.
3. Figuratively, the verb can express a malicious intent: to imagine evil, to conspire, to secretly or collectively prepare someone's ruin. It is to plot against a person.
H2050.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of violence and haste. The verb belongs to a family of words related to sudden movement and force. In Hebrew, several verbs of violent action stem from similar roots, illustrating how the language captures gestures and states of agitation: to cry out, to struggle, to assault are closely related images.
H2050.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Psalm 62:4. It is part of a scene of persecution where the psalmist laments that his enemies conspire against him, all together, to destroy him. The context is one of slander and malice: the accusers seek only to bring him down. The verb captures the collective and aggressive nature of this attack — it is not an isolated act, but a unanimous rush. That is why the psalmist takes refuge in God for protection.
H2050.portee: This word reminds the reader that human malice can be collective and overwhelming, but it does not triumph over those who trust in God. The psalmist, faced with those who throw him down, continues to proclaim his faith. The verb helps to feel the moral and physical violence of persecution, and the calm courage of the righteous who refuse to bend.

sens: A place of trade in antiquity
H2051.detail: 1. Vedan is a place or site mentioned in the Old Testament as a center of commercial exchange. The context of Ezekiel 27:19 places it among the suppliers of Tyre, the great Phoenician trading city: Vedan sends worked iron, resin (aromatic resin), and fragrant reeds. It is a place name, not a product, although some ancient commentators have read "cases" or "barrels" instead.
H2051.origine: The Hebrew word וְדָן (ve.dan) consists of the conjunction "and" (ו) followed by "Dan." The precise identity of this place remains uncertain: some scholars locate it near Medina in Arabia, while others think it should simply be read as "even Dan," another region. Its absence from the rest of the Bible and the obscurity of its exact location make it one of the enigmatic geographical names in the sacred text.
H2051.emploi: Vedan appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:19, in the great lamentation of the prophet over the fall of Tyre. This chapter lists the peoples and places that trade with Tyre, each bringing its own products. Vedan is mentioned as a supplier of precious goods (worked metals and aromatics), highlighting its role in the ancient Near Eastern trade networks. The unique mention offers little clarification on its exact geography.

sens: A place located in the territory of Moab
Region of Israel's wars against the peoples of the Desert
H2052.detail: Vaheb is a place mentioned only once in the Bible, in a quotation from the Book of the Wars of the Lord, an ancient work of which we only have excerpts. This place was located in Moab, an area east of the Jordan. The context indicates that it was a site of battles for Israel during the crossing of the Desert, before entering Canaan (Numbers 21:14).
H2052.origine: The Hebrew name Vaheb is uncommon and its exact meaning is uncertain. Some scholars link it to a root meaning "to give" or "to offer," but this remains conjectural. The name could be of Moabite origin or reflect an ancient language of the Desert.
H2052.emploi: Vaheb appears only once in the entire Bible, in Numbers 21:14. This verse cites it as part of an ancient poetry, extracted from the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which recounted Israel's military victories. The mention of Vaheb and the torrents of Arnon situates this place within the geography of Transjordan, where Israel won decisive battles during the Exodus.

sens: A piece of metal shaped like a hook or a fishhook
A fastening element used to assemble or hold together
A protruding part of a column allowing for suspension or attachment
H2053.detail:
1. A hook is a curved piece of metal, often made of gold or silver, shaped like a fishhook or a clasp. It is a concrete object intended to hang, hold, or assemble other elements. In the Tabernacle, the columns of the courtyard had gold or silver hooks, as shown in Exodus 26:32: "its columns shall have hooks of gold."
2. The hook functions as a point of attachment or connection. It allows for fixing rods or fabrics by passing through these hooks, thus creating a solid structure. In Exodus 27:10, we see how the hooks work with the columns and rods to form the enclosure of the courtyard: "the hooks of the columns and their rods shall be of silver."
3. More broadly, it is a construction and assembly element that provides stability to the whole. Each hook, though small, plays an essential role in holding the structure together: the hooks of the columns and their rods keep all the elements of the courtyard assembled and rigid.
H2053.origine: The Hebrew word vav literally means "hook" or "fishhook." Its original image is that of a curve or bending — something that wraps or holds. Interestingly, the word vav is also the name of the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ו), which has exactly this shape of a small hook. The word belongs to a semantic family expressing the idea of binding, assembling, or holding together.
H2053.emploi: The word vav appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in chapters 26 to 38 of the book of Exodus. All these uses concern the construction of the Tabernacle and its courtyard. The hooks are always fastening elements for the columns: they allow for attaching the rods and fabrics that form the enclosure. They are found on the acacia columns of the Sanctuary (Exodus 26:32, 36:36), on the columns of the courtyard with its curtains (Exodus 27:10-17, 38:10-17), or in the weight of the materials used (Exodus 38:28). The context is always technical and architectural: it aims to describe precisely how the pieces fit together. No figurative or spiritual use.
H2053.portee: This word reminds us of the extraordinary care given to every detail of the Tabernacle. A simple hook, which might seem trivial, is mentioned thirteen times because it contributes to the order and stability of God's dwelling. This teaches the believer that no detail is too small for God, and that faithfulness in the little things — the "hooks" of spiritual life — creates a solid structure of communion with the Lord.

sens: One who has committed an offense, a reprehensible act
One who bears guilt, the responsibility for a transgression
One who deviates from righteousness and innocence
H2054.detail:
1. The word designates one who has committed an offense or a reprehensible act: someone who has made themselves guilty of a transgression. It is the direct opposite of the innocent (Proverbs 21:8).
2. To be guilty is to bear guilt: a moral burden and responsibility before God. The guilty cannot ignore that they have violated a rule, a law, or the order established by the Lord.
3. The meaning extends to one who voluntarily deviates from the right path: the guilty "follows crooked paths" (Proverbs 21:8), while the innocent acts with righteousness. It is a moral judgment on the character and intentions of the person.
H2054.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of deviating, straying from the straight path. It is related to terms that designate what is strange or out of place. The basic image is that of someone who strays from the norm, the law, or the established order.
H2054.emploi: The word appears infrequently in the Old Testament. Its only use in Proverbs 21:8 contrasts the guilty with the innocent: the guilty deviates from righteousness in their actions and paths. Biblical wisdom opposes it to one who acts with integrity. This passage uses the word to morally characterize one whose conscience condemns them.
H2054.portee: This word reminds the believer that guilt is not an abstraction, but a concrete reality that manifests in the way one lives: the guilty follow crooked, hidden paths, while the one who walks in innocence acts with all righteousness. It is a call to examine one's own ways before God and to seek integrity rather than guilt.

sens: One of the ten sons of Haman
Son of the minister Haman at the court of King Ahasuerus
Executed at the same time as his father
H2055.detail: 1. Vajezatha is one of the ten sons of the minister Haman mentioned in the book of Esther (Esther 9:9). His name appears in the list of Haman's children who were condemned to death along with their father. 2. He lived during the time of the exile and the return of Israel, at the court of the Persian King Ahasuerus, where his father held a position of power before his downfall. 3. Along with his nine brothers (Parschandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmaschtha, Arisai, and Aridai), he was hanged by order of the king, thus fulfilling divine judgment against Haman's house, which had plotted the destruction of the Jews.
H2055.origine: The name Vajezatha means "strong as the wind" in Hebrew, evoking a certain vigor or strength. It fits into the list of names of Haman's sons, many of which have Persian or hybrid resonance, reflecting the historical context of the book of Esther in the Persian empire.
H2055.emploi: Vajezatha is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 9:9, where his name appears among those of his nine brothers in the list of Haman's executed sons. The context is that of the spectacular reversal of the anti-Semitic plot: Haman, who had obtained from the king a decree to annihilate the Jews, was himself hanged, along with his ten sons, according to Persian law. This mention illustrates how God's justice was exercised not only against the conspirator but against all his descendants involved in his scheme.
H2055.portee: The fate of Vajezatha and his brothers shows that God's judgment reaches not only the principal guilty party but can extend to their entire household, especially when it participates in their wicked plans. It is also a reminder of the protection that God grants to His people: even in the midst of exile, He saves His own and dramatically overturns the enemies.

sens: Young human being, from infant to adolescent
Descendant, son or daughter, in relation to their parents
Offspring
Inexperienced or immature person
H2056.detail:
1. The child is the young human in the most direct sense. The Hebrew word valad comes from the root meaning "to give birth" or "to bring forth": it is one who has just been born or who grows under the protection of their parents. In Genesis 11:30, Sarai had no children, which was a source of great distress in a culture where offspring were seen as an essential blessing.
2. By extension, child can refer to any descendant: the filial bond matters more than age. It is one who is born of parents and continues their existence and name.
3. The child can also evoke offspring, the fruit of generation, the natural heir to whom life and heritage are transmitted.
4. Figuratively, a child can be someone inexperienced, naive, or immature — one who is still unaware of the realities of the world.
H2056.origine: The word valad comes from the Hebrew root yld, which fundamentally means "to give birth," "to deliver," or "to bring forth." This root is found in words of the same family: yeled (another form of child), yalda (female child), and even in the name Jehoiada. The starting image is that of birth and generation: the child is literally one who comes out of their mother's body.
H2056.emploi: This word is attested once in the provided usages: Genesis 11:30, where it describes Sarai's lack of children before the miracle of her motherhood. It is a fundamental term in the Hebrew Bible to express the relationship of descent and the continuity of generations, at the heart of God's promises to Abram regarding an innumerable posterity. The term applies indiscriminately to son or daughter, and their absence or presence marks the significant narrative turning points in God's plan.
H2056.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the birth and life of children are gifts from God. Sarai's barrenness and her desire for a child illustrate a fundamental human aspiration, later fulfilled by divine intervention. This speaks to the importance of generational renewal in God's plan and the trust that must be placed in Him even in waiting.

sens: Jewish man during the time of the return from exile, in the time of Ezra
H2057.detail: Vania is a Jew who lived during the return from exile, after the captivity in Babylon. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:36, among the sons of Bani. Like many others at that time, he had married a foreign woman, which was against the law of Moses and caused great concern for Ezra and the leaders of the people. It was a critical moment for the preservation of the Jewish community: Ezra and the elders gathered the people to renounce these mixed marriages and separate from their foreign wives (Ezra 10:10-11). Vania appears in this list of those who accepted to comply with this requirement.
H2057.origine: The name Vania comes from the Hebrew וַנְיָה (vanyah) and means "Jehovah is praise" or "Jehovah is glory." It is composed of the divine name (Yah, a short form of Yhwh) and an element evoking praise or acclaim. This theophoric name — that is, containing the name of God — was common among the Hebrews: it proclaimed the greatness of the Lord and expressed trust in His blessing.
H2057.emploi: Vania is mentioned only once in Scripture, in Ezra 10:36. He appears in the list of men of Judah and Benjamin who had taken foreign wives at the time of the return from exile, after King Cyrus had allowed the Jews to return from Babylon (circa 538 B.C.). This historical moment was decisive: Ezra, the scribe and priest, believed that these unions threatened the religious identity of the chosen people. Vania is associated with other sons of Bani — a family group — and participated in this collective repentance. His very name, meaning praise of God, creates a poignant contrast: a man bearing a name that exalts the Lord had to publicly correct himself to remain faithful to the faith of his fathers.

sens: father of Nahbi, one of the twelve spies sent by Moses
H2058.detail: Vophsi is a man whose name appears only once in the Bible. He is the father of Nahbi, chosen by Moses as a representative of the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve spies sent to explore the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:14). Although nothing else is known about him, his son Nahbi participated in this pivotal mission that marked Israel's history in the wilderness.
H2058.origine: The Hebrew name Vophsi literally means "rich" or "abundance." It is a proper name borne by this father, whose memory has only survived through his son Nahbi, whose name means "hidden." There is no indication whether Vophsi himself participated in the events of the wilderness or if he remained in Egypt.
H2058.emploi: Vophsi is mentioned only once in Scripture: in Numbers 13:14, where Moses chooses the twelve men who will explore Canaan. The text simply designates him as the father of Nahbi, representative of the tribe of Naphtali. He is just a name in a list, but he reminds us that behind each spy was a family with its own story. Vophsi represents the generations that passed through Egypt and the wilderness, of whom we retain only fragments of memory.

sens: Son of the prophet Samuel
Levite of the united kingdom of Israel
H2059.detail: Vaschni is a son of the prophet Samuel, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:28 as Samuel's firstborn, brother of Abijah. He was a Levite living during the time of the united monarchy, before the division of the kingdom. He is the father of Heman, who became an important musician and prophet in the service of the tabernacle and temple worship.
H2059.origine: The name Vaschni means "strong" or "mighty." It designates a man from the tribe of Levi from the early period of the Israelite monarchy. The same character is also called Joel elsewhere in the Bible (see 1 Samuel 8:2), but here he bears the name Vaschni.
H2059.emploi: Vaschni appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:28, where he is explicitly named as Samuel's firstborn. Although historically significant as the son of the great prophet Samuel and father of Heman, the Bible says nothing more about him. What we know of him comes mainly from his genealogical role: he connects Samuel to Heman and shows how the spiritual responsibilities of Levitical worship were passed down through priestly families.
H2059.portee: Vaschni reminds us that behind great servants of God like Samuel are entire families committed to the service of the Lord. Although little known, his descendants (notably Heman) played a major role in Israel's worship, demonstrating how faithfulness is passed from one generation to the next.

sens: Queen of Persia, first wife of King Ahasuerus
Woman of great beauty and personal dignity
Figure of disobedience to royal authority
H2060.detail: Vasthi is the Persian queen, the first wife of King Ahasuerus (Ahasuerus being the Achaemenid king historically known as Xerxes I). She is beautiful in appearance, as noted in Esther 1:11 where the king wants to show her beauty to the peoples and the nobles. Her refusal to come at the king's command becomes the turning point of the book: when Ahasuerus orders her, through his eunuchs, to appear before the court, she flatly refuses (Esther 1:12). This refusal angers the king and creates a crisis: Memucan and the king's advisors see this act not only as personal disobedience but as one that could inspire all the women of the kingdom to despise their husbands. This political fear leads to her repudiation and the search for a new queen, which opens the door to Esther's destiny.
H2060.origine: The Hebrew name וַשְׁתִּי (Vashti) literally means "beautiful" or "desirable," according to the transmitted definition. It is a name of Persian origin that reflects the exilic context of the book of Esther, set in the royal court of Susa, the capital of the Achaemenid empire.
H2060.emploi: Vasthi appears ten times in the book of Esther, exclusively in chapter 1 and chapter 2. All instances focus on the central event: her feast parallel to that of the king (1:9), her praised beauty (1:11), her refusal to obey (1:12), the resulting political controversy (1:15-1:17), and ultimately her repudiation (1:19). The narrative in 2:1 and 2:4 shows the consequence: the search for the queen who will replace her. The book of Esther does not mention her again after this, as she disappears from the scene, making way for Esther herself (2:17).
H2060.portee: Vasthi represents a critical moment in the narrative where pride and personal conscience come into conflict with authority. Her refusal, though costly for her, demonstrates a form of dignity in the face of a humiliating demand. Her story illustrates how individual choices, even those that seem unfortunate, fit into God's larger plan: her downfall allows Esther to become queen and save her people.

sens: Wild carnivorous animal that hunts in packs
Violent and ruthless warrior or leader
Corrupt chief or judge who oppresses his people
Enemy who devours and destroys
Future state of messianic peace where predators and prey coexist
H2061.detail:
1. The wolf is a fierce predator of flocks and game in Israel and the Middle East. In Genesis 49:27, Benjamin is compared to a wolf that "tears" and "devours the prey," evoking his warrior and aggressive nature.
2. In judgment prophecies, the wolf represents the destructive violence of leaders and judges. Ezekiel 22:27 describes the leaders of Jerusalem as "wolves tearing their prey" and "shedding blood" — an image of the ruthless exploitation of the weak.
3. As an agent of divine judgment, the wolf is sent by God to punish an unfaithful people. Jeremiah 5:6 speaks of the "wolf of the desert" that destroys the inhabitants as a consequence of their numerous transgressions.
4. In Habakkuk 1:8, the Assyrian warriors move with the speed of "evening wolves" — the animal symbolizes brutal power and warrior agility.
5. In visions of messianic peace (Isaiah 11:6 and 65:25), the wolf "will dwell with the lamb" and "will graze together" — a miraculous reversal of all violence, a sign of final restoration.
H2061.origine: The Hebrew word זְאֵב (ze'ev) literally designates the wolf, a well-known animal of the ancient Levant. No certain etymology is established, but the word is found in other Semitic languages. In the Greek Old Testament, it is translated by the Greek λύκος (lukos). The image of the wolf is constant in the Bible to express ferocity and predation, both animal and human or spiritual.
H2061.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament. In Genesis 49:27, it characterizes the tribe of Benjamin as warrior-like. In the prophecies of Isaiah (11:6 and 65:25), the wolf embodies the predator whose wild nature will be transformed in the messianic age. In Jeremiah 5:6, Ezekiel 22:27, and Habakkuk 1:8, it symbolizes either the destructive violence of divine judgment or that of tyrants and conquerors. The usage of the word alternates between the literal sense (real animal) and the figurative sense (brutal power or immorality), depending on the prophetic context.
H2061.portee: The wolf reminds the reader that violence and predation have causes — unfaithfulness, injustice, transgression — and do not go unpunished. But above all, the image of the wolf lying down with the lamb in Isaiah offers a promise of hope: even the most hostile nature will be transformed by God's final intervention. It invites us to wait and believe that the violence of the present world will not have the final word.

sens: Prince of Midian killed during Gideon's victory
H2062.detail: Zeeb is one of the two princes of Midian defeated by Gideon and the Israelites. His name means "wolf" in Hebrew, an image of ferocity and danger. He is captured and killed at the winepress that will bear his name (Judges 7:25), and then becomes a biblical example of an enemy leader defeated whom God delivers into the hands of His people (Judges 8:3; Psalms 83:12).
H2062.origine: The name Zeeb literally means "wolf" in Hebrew. It is a warrior's name that evokes brutal and predatory strength — an appropriate characteristic for a prince of Midian, a nomadic people known for their warlike nature. The wolf was in Israel a symbol of danger and devastation.
H2062.emploi: Zeeb appears three times in the Bible, always in reference to his defeat. First in Judges 7:25, where he is killed at the winepress during the pursuit of the Midianites. In Judges 8:3, the men of Ephraim remind Gideon that God delivered Zeeb and his companion Oreb into their hands. Finally, in Psalms 83:12, the psalmist prays that God's enemies suffer the same fate as Zeeb and Oreb — a request that shows how their defeat has become an example of divine judgment against Israel's adversaries.
H2062.portee: The victory over Zeeb and Oreb illustrates how God gives victory to His people, even against powerful enemies. It also teaches that true power does not lie in the number or physical strength of warriors, but in faithfulness to God and His guidance.

sens: What is in front of oneself, what can be pointed at
What has just been spoken of or what is about to be announced
A thing, a fact considered in itself
A person or a reality viewed in its characteristics
A set of prescriptions or provisions
A conclusion or consequence that follows
H2063.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of direct demonstration: this or that refers to what is there, present, that can be shown. In Genesis 2:23, Adam says "This is now bone of my bones" when seeing the woman created from his own flesh — he shows her, he points out her presence and unique character. It is the gesture of the finger, the gaze that fixes.
2. Often the word refers to what has just been said or what is about to be said. In 2 Kings 19:31, "This is what the zeal of the Lord will do" summarizes a promise and affirms its certainty: "this" gathers and validates.
3. The word can also simply designate a thing, a fact, a reality considered in itself, without any particular link of proximity. In Numbers 4:19, "Do this" orders a specific and defined action.
4. Applied to a person, "this" or "that" qualifies their essence or condition. In Psalms 109:27, "It is You, Lord, who made him" affirms the identity or authority of the subject.
5. In the laws and biblical prescriptions (Leviticus 7:1, 7:11, 7:37), the word introduces or summarizes an ordinance: "this is the law", "these are the ordinances".
6. In the context of conclusion or consequence, "this" or "that" announces what must result from it or what logically follows.
H2063.origine: In biblical Hebrew, זֹאת (zot) is a singular feminine demonstrative pronoun, derived from a very ancient root expressing the idea of showing or designating. It belongs to the family of Hebrew demonstratives (zeh for masculine, éleh for plural). The word is built on a base that exists in several Semitic languages and retains the primitive image of the gesture of designation — pointing with the finger at what is there, present, and visible.
H2063.emploi: This pronoun appears about 570 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the narratives of Genesis and in the laws of Leviticus and Exodus. It is one of the most frequent words in the biblical text. In the narratives (Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, 2 Kings), it concretely designates objects, people, or events that are highlighted: the woman created (Genesis 2:23), the signs of the flood (Genesis 9:12), a city delivered (2 Kings 19:31). In the laws and prescriptions (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers), it introduces or recaps rules: "This is the law of the guilt offering" (Leviticus 7:1), "Here is what you must do" (Numbers 4:19). Its use ranges from simple pointing to highlighting a doctrine or a promise, depending on the context. It can also reinforce an affirmation ("it is You" in Psalms 109:27) or announce a consequence.
H2063.portee: For the modern reader, this pronoun teaches how the Bible speaks: it shows, it affirms, it places realities before our eyes. Each "this" or "that" in the biblical text invites us to stop and look at what is being pointed out — a beloved person, a kept promise, a law to be respected. Understanding this word is learning to read the Bible with the attention and presence it demands.

sens: To give a gift to someone, to generously provide them
To equip someone with what they need
To grant someone a favor, a grace
H2064.detail:
1. To endow means to gift, to generously give someone what they did not have. It is an act of generosity and favor: Leah exclaims, "God has given me a good gift" (Genesis 30:20), celebrating the divine grace that has granted her a sixth son.
2. The verb can also evoke the act of equipping someone, providing them with what they lack to live or succeed. It is to endow in the sense of "to provide endowment".
3. In a spiritual context, it is the favor that God freely grants to His creatures: He endows, He provides, He bestows out of pure goodwill.
H2064.origine: The Hebrew root comes from an image of bestowal, of generous transmission. It expresses the idea of giving what is necessary or precious to someone else. The word belongs to the vocabulary of interpersonal and divine relationships, especially when referring to God's benevolence towards His children.
H2064.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 30:20. Leah uses it to acknowledge that God has given her a "good gift" by giving her a sixth son. The context shows that she sees this birth not as a mere biological event, but as an act of divine grace, a generous endowment from God. This unique usage reveals the rarity of the term in sacred texts, but also its emotional and theological weight: expressing gratitude for a gift received from God.
H2064.portee: This word reminds us that all good comes from God, and that life should not be seen as a given. Leah recognizes that her children are divine gifts, graces granted. For the believer, meditating on this verb invites gratitude: what we have, our talents, our strengths, our relationships, all are an endowment that God entrusts to us. It is an invitation to receive blessings with humility and thankfulness.

sens: A present offered generally as a sign of honor or blessing
A gift given by a parent to their daughter at marriage
A visible mark of divine favor or blessing
H2065.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a present, a gift offered as a sign of esteem or blessing. It is the idea of generosity expressed concretely. 2. It can also mean the dowry that a father gives to his daughter when marrying her, which was a common practice in antiquity: thus Leah sees the child she has just given to her husband as a gift that God grants her (Genesis 30:20). 3. In this verse, the gift takes on a spiritual dimension: it is the visible mark of divine favor, the proof that God blesses Leah by granting her many sons.
H2065.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of increasing or augmenting. It is related to terms denoting wealth and abundance. It is a simple and ancient word, deeply rooted in the concrete life of Eastern family and marriage.
H2065.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 30:20. It is Leah who uses it upon seeing the birth of Zebulun, her sixth son. She calls this child a "gift" from God, expressing her joy and gratitude for the fertility that God grants her. It is a word that belongs to the vocabulary of blessing and thanksgiving.
H2065.portee: This word reminds us that all good received, especially children and descendants, is a gift from God. It teaches us gratitude: Leah recognizes in each son a proof of divine goodness towards her. It is an invitation to see in the blessings of our lives, both great and small, marks of our Father's generosity.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living during the time of the divided monarchy
H2066G.detail: Zabad is a proper name referring to a man from Judah mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe. He is the son of Nathan and the father of Ephlal, placing him in a precise genealogical line of Judah documented in 1 Chronicles 2:36-37.
H2066G.origine: The name Zabad means "he bestows" or "he enriches" in Hebrew, deriving from a root that evokes the idea of giving or providing. This meaning reflects a blessing or divine favor, a common theme in Hebrew names that express God's action toward His people.
H2066G.emploi: Zabad is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 2, in the genealogy of Judah. He appears in verse 36 as the son of Nathan, and in verse 37 as the father of Ephlal. These mentions place him within a line of descendants that connects the generations of the tribe of Judah, without any personal actions being reported.

sens: Name of a man from the tribe of Ephraim
H2066H.detail: Zabad is the name of a man mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. He is the son of Tahath and the father of Shuthelah (1 Chronicles 7:21). This name, like many Hebrew names, carries the meaning "he bestows" or "he enriches," expressing the idea of a blessing or divine generosity toward children.
H2066H.origine: The name Zabad comes from the Hebrew root zbd, which means "to bestow, enrich, provide." It is a theophoric name carrying a wish for blessing: the bearer is seen as someone whom God fills with gifts. Several men bore this name in Israel's history, showing its popularity among Hebrew families.
H2066H.emploi: The Bible mentions several men named Zabad. This one appears only in the genealogical list of the tribe of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:21. He is mentioned in a context where the genealogy enumerates the descendants of Ephraim, establishing familial links over several generations. Other Zabads are mentioned elsewhere in Scripture, including one among David's warriors, one conspiring against King Joash, and others during the time of the return from exile under Ezra.

sens: man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
one of the mighty warriors of King David
H2066I.detail: Zabad is a character from the Old Testament living during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. He appears in the account of David's warriors as one of those who served the king with valor and strength (1 Chronicles 11:41).
H2066I.origine: The name Zabad literally means "he bestows" or "he enriches," derived from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of giving or providing. This name reflects the hope or belief that this child would bring a blessing or prosperity to his family.
H2066I.emploi: Zabad is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 11:41, where he is listed among the mighty and renowned warriors who fought under King David's command. Although the text provides few details about his specific exploits, his inclusion in this list honors him as someone who distinguished himself by his courage and military skill. Several people bore this name at different periods in Israel's history (some during the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra), but the uses provided specifically target this warrior of David.

sens: Man from the family of Zattu who divorced his foreign wife during the time of Ezra
H2066J.detail: Zabad is one of the descendants of Zattu who, at the command of the prophet Ezra, repudiated his foreign wife during the period of the return from exile to Jerusalem (Ezra 10:27). His name literally means "he bestows" or "he enriches," expressing the idea of generosity or endowment.
H2066J.origine: The name Zabad comes from the Hebrew root "zaval" which means "to bestow, enrich, gratify." This root evokes the image of someone who confers a good, wealth, or endowment. The name thus carried a positive connotation of liberality in ancient Hebrew culture.
H2066J.emploi: Zabad appears only once in the biblical texts that have come down to us, in Ezra 10:27. He is mentioned as one of the men from the family of Zattu who obeyed Ezra by sending away the foreign women they had married. This event is set in the context of religious and national restoration after the Babylonian exile, a time when Jewish religious leaders sought to preserve the purity of the community and the covenant with God.

sens: Man of the return from exile
Son of Hashum
H2066K.detail: Zabad is a man living during the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. He is mentioned in the book of Ezra as one of the descendants of Hashum who had taken a foreign wife and had to send her away at the command of the prophet Ezra (Ezra 10:33).
H2066K.origine: The name Zabad means "he bestows" or "he enriches" in Hebrew, coming from a root expressing the idea of endowment. It is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, including warriors of David and ancestors during the return from exile.
H2066K.emploi: Zabad appears only once in the Segond in chapter 10 of Ezra, at the time when the prophet Ezra orders the Israelites returned from captivity to send away the foreign women they had married, as this would have contaminated the holiness of the people. Zabad is one of the many descendants of Hashum who obey this order and submit to communal correction.

sens: Man of Judah who lived during the Exile and the return
Son of Nebo who sent away his foreign wife under Ezra's order
H2066L.detail:
1. Zabad is a Judean who lived during the time of the Babylonian Exile and the return to the Promised Land, probably in the 5th century B.C. He is one of the many minor figures mentioned in the accounts of the people's reconstruction after the exile.

2. According to the account in Ezra, Zabad was one of the sons of Nebo who had married foreign women during the exile. When Ezra undertook to restore the religious purity of Israel upon their return, Zabad was among those who were convinced to send away these foreign women, thus obeying the law of Moses (Ezra 10:43).
H2066L.origine: The name Zabad means "he bestows" or "he provides" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing the idea of donation or enrichment. It is a theophoric name, like many Hebrew names, suggesting that the child is a gift from God. Several characters in the Bible bear this name, reminding us of its importance in the Israelite heritage.
H2066L.emploi: Zabad appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:43, where he is listed among the descendants of Nebo who had contracted mixed marriages. This passage is set in the context of the return from exile, when Ezra discovered that many Israelites, including priests and Levites, had married women from surrounding peoples — which was forbidden by the Law. Zabad is mentioned simply as one of those who accepted to separate from his foreign wife to remain faithful to the covenant with God.
H2066L.portee: This passage shows that even the simple faithful of the people, whose names are barely remembered, had the courage to make personal sacrifices to obey God's Word during the return from exile. The case of Zabad reminds the reader that faithfulness to God may require difficult renunciations, and that no one is exempt from this obedience — not just the great leaders, but also those who are forgotten by history.

sens: An assassin of King Joash in the 9th century B.C.
H2066M.detail: Zabad is a man from the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. He is the son of an Ammonite woman named Shimeath. Alongside Jozabad, he conspires against King Joash of Judah and kills him, according to the account in 2 Chronicles 24:26.
H2066M.origine: The name Zabad means "he provides" or "he bestows." It comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of giving or enriching. It was a common name in ancient Israel, borne by several characters in the Old Testament.
H2066M.emploi: Zabad is named only once in the Segond 1910, in 2 Chronicles 24:26, where he is presented as one of the two murderers of King Joash. He is identified as the son of Shimeath, an Ammonite woman — this detail underscores the involvement of foreigners in this crime against the monarch of Judah. His name also appears in the parallel text of 2 Kings 12:22, where he is called Jozacar.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah, father of Achan
son of Zerah and grandson of Judah
H2067G.detail: Zabdi is a man of the tribe of Judah whose name appears in the genealogy of Achan, the one who committed the sin of covetousness at the time of the conquest of Canaan. He is the direct father of Achan and the grandson of Zerah. His lineage is mentioned three times in the passage of Joshua 7, when the people of Israel are gathered by tribes, families, and households to discover the culprit of the theft of the devoted things. The Bible does not provide further information about Zabdi himself: he lived before the Israelite monarchy, and it is mainly through his grandson Achan that his name remains memorable in biblical history.
H2067G.origine: The name Zabdi means "gift" or "what is given": it comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of a gift or a portion received. It is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, but this Zabdi is especially known as the ancestor of Achan, the man whose sin brought calamity upon all Israel at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
H2067G.emploi: Zabdi appears in the book of Joshua in chapter 7, where the discovery of the theft of the devoted things is recounted. Three times, in Joshua 7:1, 7:17, and 7:18, Achan's genealogy is fully recalled: "Achan, son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah." This repetition underscores the importance of genealogical traceability within the people of God and the gravity of sin. Although Zabdi himself is not an actor in the narrative, his name is etched in the memory of Israel as that of the grandfather of the sinner whose act led to the defeat of Jericho and the death of several thousand Israelites.

sens: son of Shimei, of the tribe of Benjamin
H2067H.detail: Zabdi is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:19, where he appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. He is identified as the son of Shimei and brother of several other men: Jakim, Zichri, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath. This genealogical passage tells us little about his personal life or actions, but it reflects the importance given by the chronicles to the preservation of tribal lineages of Israel.
H2067H.origine: The name Zabdi means "gift" or "present" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of a wealth or grace received. Several people bear this name in the Old Testament: a son of Zerah and grandson of Judah (ancestor of Achan), an officer of David in charge of the vineyards, and a son of the musician Asaph (also called Zaccur or Zichri). Each of these individuals belonged to different generations and contexts, but they share the same significant name.
H2067H.emploi: Zabdi appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 8:19, in the genealogical record of the sons of Shimei. He is not the subject of a specific narrative or action: his mention simply confirms his existence within the Benjaminite genealogy. This modest place in Scripture reflects the role of biblical genealogies, which sought to establish family ties and continuity of lineages, particularly important after the exile.

sens: officer of David in charge of the vineyards and wine reserves
H2067I.detail: Zabdi is a proper name designating a man who served King David. He was responsible for the royal vineyards and the wine provisions that came from them — an important function in the administration of the kingdom, as wine was a valuable and highly controlled resource. He is encountered only once in the Bible, in the role of steward of the king's vineyards.
H2067I.origine: The name Zabdi comes from a Hebrew root meaning "gift" or "endowment" (zabdiel, "gift of God"). It is a compound name expressing the idea of a wealth given or entrusted. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, reflecting its meaning of divine blessing.
H2067I.emploi: Zabdi appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 27:27, in the list of officers that David had placed over various royal domains and resources. In this position, he represents one of the administrators of the king's estate and goods — a testament to the organized and hierarchical system of the Israelite monarchy at its peak.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi at the time of the exile and return
Son of Asaph, temple musician
H2067J.detail: Zabdi is a Levite who lived during the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem. He is known as the son of Asaph, one of the great musicians of the temple established by King David. In Nehemiah 11:17, he is mentioned as the ancestor of Mattaniah, who was the leader of the praise and directed the songs during prayers in the restored temple. The name Zabdi means "gift" or "endowment" in Hebrew, evoking a blessing or a present.
H2067J.origine: The name Zabdi comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to give" or "present." It expresses the idea of an endowment or divine blessing. The source definition mentions that Zabdi may be another name for Zichri (זִכְרִי), suggesting the existence of variations in the transmission of Levitical proper names. This name belonged to important members of the tribe of Levi, associated with the worship and music of the temple.
H2067J.emploi: Zabdi is mentioned only once in the Bible translated by the Segond: in Nehemiah 11:17. He appears there in a genealogy of Levites who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is presented as the father of Micah and grandfather of Mattaniah. Mattaniah, his grandson, occupies a prominent role: he is the leader who "begins the praise at prayer," indicating that he leads the liturgical singing in the temple. This passage shows the importance of Zabdi's family line in the restoration of worship in Jerusalem.
H2067J.portee: The mention of Zabdi illustrates how God preserves the families of faithful servants through the exile and return. His grandson Mattaniah becomes a leader of praise, showing that the musical and liturgical vocation is passed down within the people of God.
