This encourages the believer to see how God maintains His worship and presence, even in times of captivity and restoration.

sens: Father of Jaschobeam, chief of David's guard
H2068G.detail: Zabdiel is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Jaschobeam, an important warrior in the service of King David. Jaschobeam commanded the first division of the royal army, composed of twenty-four thousand men, which shows that he held a high position of trust with the king. Zabdiel himself appears in biblical history only to make known this familial connection (1 Chronicles 27:2).
H2068G.origine: The name Zabdiel means "God is my endowment" or "God is my gift." It is composed of Hebrew roots: "zabad" (to give, to endow) and "El" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries an affirmation of faith in the God of Israel, like many Hebrew names from ancient times.
H2068G.emploi: Zabdiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:2. There he is designated as the father of Jaschobeam, who is presented as the chief of the first division of David's army. This passage is part of an administrative list of officers and military divisions of King David, suggesting that Zabdiel belonged to a family of military and political importance in the united kingdom of Israel. His brief appearance in this context of prestige indicates that he was a notable figure.

sens: Priest during the time of Nehemiah, leader of his fellow priests
H2068H.detail: Zabdiel is a priest living in the time of Nehemiah (around the fifth century B.C.), after the return from exile in Babylon. He is designated as the leader of a group of one hundred twenty-eight "valiant men," his brothers in the priesthood — that is, priests recognized for their faithfulness and spiritual strength (Nehemiah 11:14). His name means "God is my provision" or "God is my inheritance," which is perfectly fitting for a priest of God in restored Israel.
H2068H.origine: The name Zabdiel comes from two Hebrew roots: *zabad*, which means "to bestow" or "to grant," and *El*, which refers to God. It expresses the idea that God Himself is the provision or inheritance of the bearer of the name — a profound theme for priests, who had no land of their own but considered God and His service as their portion.
H2068H.emploi: Zabdiel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:14. It is a list of the priests and Levites who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. Zabdiel is mentioned as the son of Gedolim and as the leader of a group of "valiant" priests — a phrase that emphasizes their dedication and moral strength in the rebuilding of the religious community of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Beriah
H2069G.detail: Zebadja is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:15. He is the son of Beriah and the brother of Arad, Eder, and others. His name means "gift of the Lord" in Hebrew, expressing gratitude to God for this son. This genealogical passage shows us the descendants of Benjamin and the importance that Scripture attaches to the transmission of names and family lines.
H2069G.origine: The name Zebadja is composed of two Hebrew elements: "zébad" (gift, present) and "yah" (a contraction of the divine name Jehovah). It literally means "gift of Jehovah" or "the Lord has given." It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, where parents expressed their trust in God by naming their children this way.
H2069G.emploi: Zebadja appears only in 1 Chronicles 8:15, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. He is presented as the son of Beriah, which places him historically at the time of Egypt and the wilderness according to tradition. Although mentioned briefly, his name appears in the sacred genealogies, showing that even minor figures in biblical history have their place in the divine plan.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H2069H.detail: 1. Zebadja is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:17. He is the son of Elpaal and the brother of several other Benjamites, including Meshullam, Hizki, and Heber.
H2069H.origine: The name Zebadja means "gift of Yahweh" or "God has given": it combines two Hebrew elements expressing divine gift. This name reflects faith in God's generosity toward His creation and His descendants.
H2069H.emploi: Zebadja appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 8:17, in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. This man has no other biblical significance than to appear in this genealogical list: no actions, no events of his life are reported. Several other people bear this name in the Bible (notably a warrior of David, a priest during the time of Ezra, a Levite during the time of Jehoshaphat), but this Zebadja is simply an ancestor of the tribe.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Jeroham of Gedor
Warrior who joined David
H2069I.detail:
1. Zébadia is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, from the family of Jeroham of Gedor. He is mentioned with his brother Joela in 1 Chronicles 12:7, where he appears in the list of ancestors of this Benjaminite branch.
2. Zébadia is one of the warriors who rally to David, according to 1 Chronicles 12:7. His name appears in the context of the warriors who come to join David, probably at the time when he is fleeing or at the beginning of his reign.
H2069I.origine: The name Zébadia means "gift of the Lord" or "endowment of the Lord." It is formed from two Hebrew elements: "zébad" (gift) and "yah" (the Lord). This name expresses gratitude to God for the child received as a divine gift, a common practice in the Bible.
H2069I.emploi: Zébadia is a historical figure of the united kingdom, mentioned only once in the historical books. He appears only in 1 Chronicles 12:7, in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin and among the warriors who join David. Although not detailed, this passage situates him at an important time in Israel's history, that of the formation of Davidic power and the consolidation of the kingdom under David.

sens: Son of Meshelemiah, gatekeeper of the temple during the reign of King David
H2069J.detail: 1. Zébadia is a Levite, a member of the Korahite family (descendants of Korah), assigned to guard the gates of the temple in Jerusalem. He is the third son of Meshelemiah and serves in his role during the reign of King David, as shown by the official enumeration of the temple gatekeepers in 1 Chronicles 26:2.
H2069J.origine: The name Zébadia means "endowment of Jehovah" or "gift of Yahweh" in Hebrew: it combines the root "zabad" (to give, to grant) and the divine Yah. It is a theophoric name — a name that contains the name of God — very common in ancient Israel to express divine blessing upon the bearer. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament.
H2069J.emploi: Zébadia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:2, where he is listed among the sons of Meshelemiah, the chief of the temple gatekeepers. He is presented as the third son in birth order. This passage is part of an administrative list from the reign of David that organizes the Levites and gatekeepers for the service of the sanctuary.

sens: Military officer under King David, son of Asahel
H2069K.detail: Zebadia is the son of Asahel and the nephew of Joab, two renowned warriors during the reign of King David. He is mentioned as the commander of a division of the royal army: he leads twenty-four thousand men during the fourth month of the year, in the administrative and military organization established by David (1 Chronicles 27:7).
H2069K.origine: The name Zebadia means "gift of God" or "endowment of the Lord" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: zébad (gift, provision) and Yah (God). This name expresses the belief that this child is a gift received from God.
H2069K.emploi: Zebadia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:7. He is presented as the son of Asahel and an officer in David's army, responsible for the contingent of the fourth month. His role fits into the administrative and military system that David had established to govern Israel and defend the kingdom.

sens: Levite serving in the temple under King Jehoshaphat of Judah
H2069L.detail: Zébadia is a Levite sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in the cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 17:8). He is part of an official delegation including other Levites and priests, tasked with religious instruction in the kingdom. This role shows his status as a minister of worship and his involvement in the religious reform initiated by this king.
H2069L.origine: The name Zébadia means "gift of Yahweh" or "Yahweh has given." It comes from two Hebrew elements: zébad (gift, present) and Yah (abbreviation of Yahweh, the name of God in Hebrew). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for a child or a blessing.
H2069L.emploi: Zébadia appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He is mentioned as one of the Levites chosen by King Jehoshaphat for a mission of religious teaching in Judah, probably around the 9th century B.C. This passage testifies to the importance that this king placed on instruction in the Law of God, and Zébadia represents those servants of worship involved in this reform.
H2069L.portee: The name Zébadia reminds us that forgotten men of history have played important roles in the religious life of Israel. His commitment as a teacher of the Law under Jehoshaphat invites Christians to recognize the importance of humble service and the faithful transmission of God's Word, even when all details are not known.

sens: Son of Ishmael, prince of the house of Judah during the reign of Jehoshaphat
H2069M.detail: Zebadiah is a figure from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 19:11, where King Jehoshaphat appoints him as chief of the house of Judah, responsible for the king's affairs. He works alongside the high priest Amaria, who oversees religious matters. Zebadiah thus fulfills an important role as a royal administrator, representing the king's authority in judicial and governmental matters of the kingdom of Judah.
H2069M.origine: The name Zebadiah means "endowment of Jehovah" or "gifted by the Lord." It is composed of two elements: a word meaning "gift" or "endowment" and the divine name "Yah" (a short form of Jehovah). This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel, expressing the recognition that all blessings and gifts come from God.
H2069M.emploi: Zebadiah appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 19:11. He is a historical figure from the 9th century BC, living during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. At that time, Jehoshaphat reorganized the administration and justice of his kingdom by establishing a division of responsibilities: Amaria managed religious affairs as high priest, while Zebadiah oversaw the civil and judicial matters of the king. His presence in the text illustrates the administrative structure of the kingdom of Judah and the importance of the balance between religious authority and civil power.

sens: A man from the tribe of Benjamin or a Levite who lived during the time of exile and return from exile
H2069N.detail: Zebadiah is a proper name borne by several important figures in the history of Israel, including descendants of Benjamin, Levites, and officials under the kings David and Jehoshaphat. The Zebadiah mentioned in Ezra 8:8 is the son of Michael, of the lineage of Shephatiah, and returns from exile in Babylon with Ezra, leading eighty men of his family.
H2069N.origine: The name Zebadiah means "gift of the Lord" or "gifted by the Lord": it is formed from two Hebrew elements, zebad ("gift, endowment") and Yah (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, very common among the Israelites to express their faith in divine generosity.
H2069N.emploi: Zebadiah is a name borne by at least nine different characters mentioned in the Old Testament: Benjamites, Levites, military officers of David, and magistrates of King Jehoshaphat. The unique usage in Ezra 8:8 refers to the one who returns from Babylonian captivity with the priest Ezra, probably in the 5th century BC. This Zebadiah is the father of eighty men of his household, indicating his importance and authority within the returning community.

sens: A priest from the family of Immer during the time of Ezra
H2069O.detail: Zebadias is a priest from the family of Immer mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile. He was among those who had married foreign women and had to send away their wives to comply with the Law (Ezra 10:20). His name, which means "God has bestowed" or "gift of God," reflects the trust that his parents placed in the Lord.
H2069O.origine: The name Zebadias comes from the Hebrew זְבַד (zevad), which means "gift" or "present," and from יָה (yah), a contraction of the divine name Yahweh. It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the name of God, expressing the idea that the child was a gift from God to his parents.
H2069O.emploi: Zebadias appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 10:20, during the religious reform led by Ezra upon the return from Babylonian exile. At that time, the leaders of Israel had allowed some of their compatriots to marry foreign women, which violated the Mosaic Law. Zebadias, as a priest, had committed this offense. The text only mentions his name in the list of those who renounced these mixed marriages, without providing further details about his life.

sens: Small flying insect with transparent wings, common and bothersome
Insignificant or harmful creature that spoils things
Enemy or plague sent by God to afflict a people
H2070.detail:
1. The fly is primarily the ordinary insect that everyone knows: small, agile, attracted to organic substances. In Ecclesiastes 10:1, even a few dead flies are enough to completely spoil the precious oil of a perfumer — a striking image to show how a small insignificant thing can ruin something great and valuable.
2. This small insect represents what is vain, futile, or destructive. A dead fly weighs nothing, but it can spoil everything: this is how Ecclesiastes uses it to show how "a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor" (Ecclesiastes 10:1).
3. In Isaiah 7:18, God promises to "whistle for the flies that are at the ends of the streams of Egypt" as a plague, a scourge He will send to afflict the enemies of Israel, in the manner of the ten plagues of Egypt.
H2070.origine: The Hebrew word זְבוּב (zebûb) simply means the fly. It is a simple, onomatopoeic word: it somewhat imitates the buzzing of the insect. This word also appears in the name "Baal-Zebub" (Matthew 12:24 in Greek Beelzebul), "the lord of the flies," a nickname given to the prince of demons — perhaps because flies are associated with decay and filth.
H2070.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Ecclesiastes 10:1, it illustrates a moral truth: tiny details can ruin everything. In Isaiah 7:18, flies are among the humiliating creatures that Egypt and Assyria will suffer as divine punishment. In both cases, it is an ordinary creature elevated to the role of a symbol: from the detail that ruins to the plague that humiliates.
H2070.portee: The dead fly of Qoheleth reminds us of a humble lesson: we are not immune to small things ruining us. It invites moral vigilance and practical wisdom. In Isaiah, it shows us that God even uses the most humble creatures to accomplish His purposes — nothing escapes His plan, not even a fly.

sens: One of the high officials of King Solomon
H2071.detail: Zabud is a historical figure mentioned only once in the Bible. He was a man who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel, specifically during the reign of King Solomon. According to 1 Kings 4:5, Zabud was the son of the prophet Nathan and brother of Azariah. He held a prestigious position at the royal court: that of "minister of state, favorite of the king." This role, called in Hebrew "friend of the king," was a position of trust that placed Zabud close to the king as a leading advisor.
H2071.origine: The name Zabud means "given" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of generosity, of what is conferred or offered. This name suits a man to whom the king had "given" an honorable charge.
H2071.emploi: Zabud appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:5. He is mentioned in the list of high officials of King Solomon, alongside other important administrators like Azariah, son of the same Nathan. This unique presence in an inventory of royal dignitaries shows the importance of his role at court, even though Scripture does not report any specific acts concerning him.

sens: Habitation, lieu de résidence
Sanctuary or temple, divine dwelling
Final abode, refuge
H2073.detail:
1. Dwelling, place of residence: the word primarily designates the place where someone lives, their home or house. In 1 Kings 8:13, Solomon states that the Temple is the dwelling where God will reside forever — it is the house, the building constructed for God.
2. Sanctuary or temple, divine dwelling: in a religious context, "dwelling" takes on the meaning of a sacred place, the house of God. In Isaiah 63:15, the "holy and glorious dwelling" of heaven refers to the place where God resides, His heavenly sanctuary — a place of power and majesty.
3. Final abode, refuge: the word can also evoke a permanent refuge or a lasting stay. In Psalms 49:15, the abode of the dead becomes the dwelling of the wicked — it is their final destination, the place where they will remain.
H2073.origine: The Hebrew word zevul comes from a root that expresses the idea of exaltation and height. The name reflects the image of an elevated, noble, remarkable place — a dwelling worthy of the name. This connotation of height and dignity characterizes the contexts in which the word appears: the dwelling of God is exalted, separate from the ordinary world.
H2073.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate an important dwelling or abode. It primarily qualifies the Temple, the house built for God (1 Kings 8:13 and 2 Chronicles 6:2 — two identical accounts). It also applies to heaven, the heavenly and holy dwelling of God (Isaiah 63:15). Finally, it can evoke a place of lasting stay, even negative: the abode of the dead for the wicked (Psalms 49:15). Each time, it is a permanent, established place that deserves the name of dwelling.
H2073.portee: This word reminds the reader that God dwells — He is not distant or abstract. The Temple built for Him is a real, visible dwelling, a focal point for encountering Him. At the same time, His dwelling is exalted, heavenly, holy — it surpasses all that humans build. The word invites recognition of where God resides and encourages communion with Him in this space of holiness.

sens: Son of Jacob and Leah
Tribe of Israel descended from Zebulun
Territory assigned to the tribe of Zebulun in Canaan
H2074.detail:
1. Zebulun is the tenth son of Jacob and the sixth child that Leah bore him. Leah names him saying: "God has given me a good gift" (Genesis 30:20), for the name means "exalted." He has brothers Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, and Issachar (his half-brothers being Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, and Benjamin).
2. The tribe of Zebulun is the collective descendants of Zebulun. During the census in the wilderness, it counts fifty-seven thousand four hundred men (Numbers 1:31). This tribe plays an active role in the wars of Israel, notably under the judges Deborah and Barak (Judges 4:6; 5:18).
3. The land of Zebulun is the region of Canaan that God assigns to this tribe (Joshua 19:10-16). Located in Galilee, it extends from the Sea of Galilee westward and southward. Several important cities like Jokneam are given to the Levites there (Joshua 21:34).
H2074.origine: The name Zebulun means "exalted" in Hebrew. It comes from a word that expresses the idea of rising up, being elevated — the image is one of ascent or dignity granted. Leah chooses this name to celebrate that her husband Jacob "will dwell with me," meaning she will have a place of honor in the household.
H2074.emploi: The name Zebulun appears about forty-three times in the Bible. It first designates the son of Jacob at his birth (Genesis 30:20), then it appears in the genealogical lists of Jacob's twelve sons (Genesis 35:23; Exodus 1:3). The tribe of Zebulun is then mentioned during the censuses in the wilderness (Numbers 1:30-31), in Moses' blessings (Deuteronomy 33:18), and in the division of the land of Canaan (Joshua 19:10-34). It actively participates in conflicts against Israel's enemies, particularly during the time of the judges (Judges 4:6; 5:18). The name also designates the tribal territory itself, which extends in northern Galilee.
H2074.portee: Zebulun reminds the believer that each member of God's people has a place and dignity. His name, which means "exalted," resonates with the idea that God honors those He chooses. The history of this tribe, active and faithful in the Lord's wars, shows how a community can stand alongside God and His prophets to fight against injustice.

sens: Member of the tribe of Zebulun
Descendant of Zebulun, son of Jacob and Leah
H2075.detail:
1. Zebulunite designates a man or woman belonging to the tribe of Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The term applies to all members of this tribe, whether they lived during the time of the patriarchs or in the era of the judges. In Numbers 26:27, the Zebulunites are counted during the second census in the wilderness: sixty-five hundred warriors.
2. More generally, it refers to a descendant of Zebulun, the tenth son of Jacob and Leah. This ancestor gave his name to his entire lineage. The Bible uses this term to quickly identify to which tribal family an individual belongs, such as Elon who was "of Zebulun" and became a judge in Israel (Judges 12:11-12).
H2075.origine: Zebulunite comes from the name Zebulun (Hebrew זְבוּלֻן), which means "dwelling" or "habitation." The name was given by Leah to her tenth son, as she said: "God has given me a good gift" (Genesis 30:20). The suffix -ite (in Hebrew -י, "i") forms an adjective of filiation: it means "belonging to" or "coming from." It is the same formation as Judite, Reubenite, or Simeonite for the other tribes.
H2075.emploi: The term Zebulunite appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first encountered in Numbers 26:27, during the census of the tribes in the wilderness of Sinai, where the Zebulunites form one of the twelve divisions of the people. It then appears in Judges 12:11-12 to designate Elon, a judge of Israel from the tribe of Zebulun. The word serves to situate a character within the tribal organization of Israel and to identify their family heritage.
H2075.portee: The name Zebulunite reminds the reader that the people of Israel were organized according to the twelve sons of Jacob, each becoming a tribe with its lands and responsibilities. This highlights the importance of heritage and tribal identity in the Old Testament: every Israelite knew where they came from and to which great family they belonged.

sens: To kill an animal as an offering to God
To present a victim at the sanctuary for God to accept
To perform an act of worship and adoration towards the Lord
To renew one's covenant with God through a communal meal
To turn to God in an important circumstance
H2076.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical act of killing or sacrificing an animal intended for offering — sheep, goat, ox, or other victims. It is a precise and solemn act: in Genesis 31:54, Jacob "offered a sacrifice on the mountain," meaning he killed the sacrificial animal.
2. The sacrifice is then presented at the sanctuary or on the altar, before the Lord, according to an established ritual. In Leviticus 17:5, the Israelites must bring their victims "to the entrance of the tent of meeting" to "offer to the Lord as sacrifices of thanksgiving" — not just anywhere, but at the consecrated place.
3. The offering becomes an act of worship and dependence on God, a way to acknowledge His authority and seek His favor. In 1 Samuel 1:3, a man goes up each year to Shiloh "to offer sacrifices" to the Lord of hosts.
4. The sacrifice can also seal a covenant or create communion: after killing it, the meat is shared in a communal meal, as in Genesis 31:54 where Jacob and his brothers "ate... and spent the night on the mountain."
5. It is a gesture made in significant circumstances — at the beginning of a reign, in times of danger, to ask for help, or to give thanks — as a means of turning to God with seriousness and commitment.
H2076.origine: The Hebrew verb זָבַח comes from a root that fundamentally means "to split, cut, slice" — the image of the sword or knife that kills. It has specialized in the religious realm to denote the ritual act of slaughtering a victim. The word is common throughout the Hebrew Bible and remains very alive: the corresponding noun (זֶבַח zébah, "sacrifice") appears about 150 times. This act was at the heart of Israel's religious life, from the patriarchal era to the Temple in Jerusalem.
H2076.emploi: The verb appears 127 times in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis to Chronicles, especially in the historical and law books. It first describes the sacrifices of the patriarchs (Genesis, with Jacob who "offered a sacrifice"), then enriches in the Law of Sinai, where it enumerates the prescribed sacrifices and their conditions (Leviticus, Deuteronomy). It then recounts the daily sacrifices at the Temple, royal celebrations, and offenses (sacrificing to false gods). The meaning sharpens according to the context: "to offer sacrifice" for the complete and ritual act, "to kill" or "to slaughter" when the emphasis is on the slaughtering, "to sacrifice" in a more general sense. In Psalms 54:8, the offering becomes a sign of heartfelt recognition: "I will willingly offer sacrifices to You."
H2076.portee: For the believer today, this word reminds us that the relationship with God requires a real cost and a concrete commitment — one cannot approach the Lord with empty hands or a distracted heart. Although animal sacrifices ended with Jesus Christ (whose unique sacrifice replaces all others), the principle remains: coming before God means giving oneself, offering what costs us, accepting transformation. The word also invites reflection on what the sacrifice of Christ on the cross represents — the Lamb of God delivered for our salvation.

sens: The act of offering an animal or a commodity to God during a religious ceremony.
A material offering that is burned, shared, or consumed to establish or maintain a covenant with the Lord.
An act of public or private worship, accompanied by prayers, expressing adoration, gratitude, or a plea for forgiveness.
The practice of eating together the meat of the offering as a sacred meal.
A biblical image of a total self-giving, where the material offering signifies the heart offered to God.
H2077.detail:
1. The sacrifice is primarily the material act of offering to God a victim (ox, sheep, goat, or other animal) or a commodity. When Jacob arrives at Genuzim, he offers a sacrifice on the mountain and invites his relatives to eat together (Genesis 31:54): it is both a religious act and a shared meal.
2. In the time of Leviticus, the sacrifice takes on various and codified forms: the sacrifice of thanksgiving includes rams, male goats, and lambs (Numbers 7:53), each animal being chosen according to the nature of the worship rendered.
3. The sacrifice primarily expresses an act of worship: to adore the Lord, to thank Him for His graces, to ask for His forgiveness, or simply to honor the covenant made with Him. The prescriptions of Leviticus describe how to burn certain parts as a fragrant offering, and how to share the rest in a sacred meal.
4. Eating together the meat of the sacrifice holds spiritual significance: sharing this meal means entering into communion with God and with the community of the people. Anyone who would eat the flesh of the sacrifice of thanksgiving in a state of impurity would render themselves unworthy and would be cut off from their people (Leviticus 7:20).
5. For the faith of Israel, the slaughtered animal represents much more than its flesh: it is the offering of the faithful's heart, their commitment to live for the Lord, their desire to reconcile or give thanks. The image is that of a life fully given to God.
H2077.origine: The Hebrew word זֶבַח (zébach) comes from a root that means "to slaughter, to butcher." It denotes the complete act: the slaughter of the victim and the resulting offering. This word is used in all the historical and legislative books of the Hebrew Bible to describe the practices of Israelite worship. In Greek, the Septuagint often translates it as θυσία (thysia), which carries the same meaning.
H2077.emploi: The word zébach appears about 153 times in the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in the legislative books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) where the rules of sacrifice are enumerated: the types of victims, the priests authorized to offer them, the portions reserved for the clergy. It also appears in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) when it is reported that a king or a faithful person offers a sacrifice at the temple. In the Psalms and the Prophets, the word takes on a moral coloring: the Lord only accepts the sacrifice if the heart of the faithful is right (see the sword of the Lord covered with fat and blood of lambs at Bozrah, Isaiah 34:6). The context varies: sacrifice of thanksgiving, covenant sacrifice, Passover, annual offerings, each having its precise meaning in Mosaic worship.
H2077.portee: For the Christian reader, the sacrifice of the Old Testament opens the understanding of the ultimate sacrifice of Christ on the Cross. Understanding what a sacrifice was in Israel — the material cost, the act of faith, the fraternal communion it created — helps to grasp why Jesus is called "the Lamb of God." This word also invites the believer to meditate on their own "living offering" to God: how their entire life becomes an act of worship and recognition.

sens: One of the two kings of Midian who invaded Israel
A king defeated and killed by Gideon
H2078.detail:
1. Zébach is one of the two Midianite kings (along with Tsalmunna) who led a great invasion against Israel. He commanded a vast army that remained at about 15,000 men after 120,000 warriors had been killed (Judges 8:10).
2. Gideon pursued him and eventually captured him along with his companion Tsalmunna at Karkor (Judges 8:12), before executing both kings, thus fulfilling vengeance for the murder of his brothers (Judges 8:21).
H2078.origine: The name means in Hebrew "deprived of protection" or "sacrificed." It designates an adversary whom God delivers defenseless to the one He has chosen to deliver His people. Zébach and his companion represent the enemies of God, delivered to judgment.
H2078.emploi: Zébach appears 9 times in Hebrew, solely in the account of Gideon (Judges 8) and a reference in Psalm 83:12. He is a historical king of Midian, mentioned as early as Judges 8:5 as the object of Gideon's pursuit. The people of Succoth refuse to help Gideon until Zébach is captured (Judges 8:6), but Gideon promises to punish them once victory is achieved (Judges 8:7). The last usage (Judges 8:15) shows Gideon confronting the people of Succoth by presenting the defeated Zébach and Tsalmunna.

sens: Man of Israel during the Exile and Return
H2079G.detail: Zabbaï is an Israelite who lived at the time when the Jews were returning from exile in Babylon. His name appears in the list of the descendants of Bebai who had married foreign women and who, at the command of Ezra, had to separate from them (Ezra 10:28). This is a concrete example of the difficult challenges that the Jews returning from exile had to face in order to preserve the purity of their community.
H2079G.origine: The name Zabbaï means "pure" in Hebrew. It expresses a quality of innocence or purity, which is remarkable for a man whose biblical story highlights the mixed marriage, a situation considered impure according to the Law.
H2079G.emploi: Zabbaï appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:28, in the list of men of Israel who had taken foreign wives during the Exile or shortly thereafter. He is mentioned among the sons of Bebai, a large family whose several members are listed in this same account. His name appears without any particular comment, simply as one of the men who had to face the strict religious demands of Ezra regarding marriage.

sens: Woman of the Judean royalty in the 7th century B.C.
H2080.detail: Zebudda is the wife of King Josiah and the mother of King Jehoiakim, two important monarchs of the kingdom of Judah. She is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the introduction of Jehoiakim: "His mother was named Zebudda, daughter of Pedahiah, of Rumah" (2 Kings 23:36). Her name indicates that she came from a family of high rank, as her father Pedahiah and her city of origin, Rumah, are specified.
H2080.origine: The name Zebudda means "given" in Hebrew, as if she had been a gift from God. It expresses the action of giving or offering, reminding us that in biblical thought, children and wives are blessings granted by the Lord.
H2080.emploi: Zebudda appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 23:36, during the enumeration of the kings of Judah. She is identified as the wife of Josiah and the mother of Jehoiakim, whose reign is situated at the beginning of the 6th century B.C. This seemingly brief mention underscores the importance of tracing the genealogy of kings and the role that royal mothers played in dynastic succession.

sens: A man of the people of Israel during the Exile and Return
H2081.detail: Zébina is an Israelite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the people were returning from exile in Babylon. He is one of the sons of Nebo who had married a foreign woman (Ezra 10:43). During the religious reform led by Ezra, these mixed marriages had to be dissolved so that the people could maintain their religious purity and identity.
H2081.origine: The name Zébina means "bought" in Hebrew. It belongs to those biblical names that carry the memory of an action or a significant circumstance related to the life of the father or mother at the time of birth.
H2081.emploi: Zébina appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:43. He is listed among a long list of Israelite men who had taken foreign wives during the exile or after the return to Jerusalem. This list is drawn up in the context of the great reform led by Ezra to restore the religious separation of Israel from neighboring peoples and to remind the people of their covenant with God.

sens: To reside somewhere, to dwell
To settle with someone with honor or dignity
To occupy an important place
H2082.detail:
1. To dwell means to reside, to have one's home in a place. It is simply to be present and to remain somewhere durably. In Genesis 30:20, Leah says that her husband "will dwell" with her, meaning he will live with her, that he will be her life companion.
2. The word also carries the idea of settling with someone with a certain prestige or recognized dignity. To dwell is not just to be physically present; it is also to occupy a place of value.
3. By extension, the word can evoke the idea of occupying a high position or being established in honor, as when one "dwells" as a master in a place, or imposes oneself there with authority.
H2082.origine: The verb zabal comes from a root that expresses the idea of remaining and settling. The family of this word in Hebrew maintains a connection with honor and dignity: to dwell somewhere also means to be recognized there, to have one's place. The word is rare in the Bible, which makes each use particularly meaningful. Its origin emphasizes the link between the act of dwelling and being established in a position of respect.
H2082.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible: in Genesis 30:20. Leah, after giving birth to her sixth son by Jacob, gives thanks by saying: "God has given me a good gift; this time my husband will dwell with me." Its unique usage shows that it is a solemn word, chosen to express not only physical cohabitation but also the establishment of the husband with his wife in a lasting and honorable relationship. It is a word of confidence: Leah hopes that Jacob, as the father of six sons, will now recognize his place with her.
H2082.portee: This word reminds us that to dwell is never neutral in the Bible: to remain somewhere is to be established and recognized there. For the Christian, this evokes the biblical idea of finding one's place, a stable dwelling with God and in the community. It is also an invitation not to remain a stranger to the world or to family, but to take root there with dignity and responsibility.

sens: Governor of Shechem under the authority of Abimelech
H2083.detail: Zebul is the administrative and military chief of the city of Shechem during the period of the Judges, appointed by Abimelech to exercise his power there. His name means "exalted" or "elevated," which suits his rank as governor. In the five verses that mention him, he appears as the right-hand man of Abimelech: he defends his master's authority against the criticisms of Gaal (Judges 9:28, 9:30), he reports to Abimelech the seditious words of Gaal (Judges 9:30), he mocks Gaal when he sees Abimelech's army approaching (Judges 9:36, 9:38), and finally, he drives Gaal out of the city to restore order (Judges 9:41).
H2083.origine: The Hebrew name זְבֻל (Zebul) derives from a root meaning "to elevate" or "to exalt." It is a theophoric or honorific name, common in ancient Near Eastern societies to designate a person of high rank. The name reflects Zebul's very function: a "high" governor above the other inhabitants of Shechem.
H2083.emploi: Zebul appears only in the account of chapter 9 of Judges, which narrates the revolt of the people of Shechem against Abimelech and the intervention of Gaal. These five occurrences (Judges 9:28, 9:30, 9:36, 9:38, 9:41) form a coherent whole: Zebul is first presented as Abimelech's commissioner (or governor), then as the one who hears the seditious words of Gaal and denounces his rebellion to Abimelech, next as the mocking spokesperson who belittles Gaal in view of the army, and finally as the one who executes Gaal's expulsion from the city. Zebul embodies the loyalty of the colonial administration to its master Abimelech in the face of local rebellion.
H2083.portee: The character of Zebul illustrates how political power can rest on trusted men who carry out the will of a leader. His role also emphasizes that revolts against the established order encounter organized resistance. For the Christian reader, Zebul shows how authority, even human and fallible, is exercised through concrete intermediaries, and how personal loyalty can support a regime, whether just or unjust.

sens: To acquire, procure something through purchase or exchange
To obtain or win in a competition or effort
To seek to obtain or accumulate (time, space, an advantage)
H2084.detail:
1. The primary meaning is "to buy" or "to acquire": it is to obtain something by paying for it or exchanging it. This verb evokes the common commercial action of procuring a good.

2. By extension, "to gain" means to obtain or accumulate something immaterial, such as time or an advantage. In Daniel 2:8, the king reproaches the magicians for wanting to "gain time" — that is, to delay the moment of responding, seeking to buy themselves time to invent an answer. The word emphasizes the tactical intention of someone trying to give themselves extra time to act or think.
H2084.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of acquiring or procuring. In biblical Hebrew, related verbs express buying and commercial exchange. The Aramaic of Daniel uses this simple form (P'al) to describe the action of "gaining" or obtaining, in the sense of procuring something for oneself.
H2084.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament (Daniel 2:8), at the heart of a dramatic scene. King Nebuchadnezzar, furious that the magicians do not recount his dream, accuses them of trying to "gain time" by evading. The context shows that "to gain" here does not mean "to obtain legitimately" but rather "to evade by accumulating delays" — a roundabout way to postpone the trial. This meaning reveals how even a simple verb can take on a nuance of malice depending on the context.
H2084.portee: This passage teaches the importance of honesty and courage in the face of authority. Trying to "gain time" through cunning is a lack of sincerity that the wise must avoid. The text invites the reader to integrity: not to attempt to evade or circumvent the truth through schemes.

sens: Outer covering of the grape berry
H2085.detail: 1. The grape skin is the covering that encases the fruit of the vine. It is a part of the grape that the Nazarites were forbidden to consume, just like the seeds, because it comes directly from the vine (Numbers 6:4). The term thus refers to a product of the vine in the strict sense, unprocessed.
H2085.origine: The Hebrew word zag specifically denotes the skin or rind of the grape. Its root evokes the idea of what envelops or covers. The context of Numbers 6:4 shows that it is a well-defined part of the fruit, significant enough to be mentioned alongside the seeds among the prohibitions of the Nazirite vow.
H2085.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 6:4, in the list of restrictions imposed on the Nazarites during their vow. This enumeration ("from the seeds to the grape skin") shows that the prohibition applies to all elements of the grape without exception: the text seeks to demonstrate the comprehensiveness of abstaining from any product of the vine, with the Nazarite being unable to consume anything, even what seems trivial.
H2085.portee: The detail of this prohibition reveals the nature of the Nazirite vow: it is not a simple abstinence, but a total commitment to separation from the fruits of the world. That the text even enumerates the minimal parts of the grape (seeds, skin) teaches the believer that consecration to God is demanding in its details and calls for constant vigilance, without compromise.

sens: One who believes themselves superior to others, contemptuous and insolent
Who acts with haughty pride, without respect for others
Who rebels against the established order, laws, or divine authority
Character of a person filled with presumptuous pride
H2086.detail:
1. The proud one is one who displays visible arrogance: they believe themselves superior and show it through their contempt for others. In Proverbs 21:24, the proud one "is called a scoffer" and "acts with the fury of arrogance," revealing how their pride manifests through ridicule and violence.
2. It is also an attitude of insolent height, a refusal to respect others. The proud of Psalms 119:69 "imagine falsehoods against me," showing how arrogance leads to malice and betrayal.
3. The word designates those who rebel against God and His law: the proud of Psalms 119:85 "dig pits" against the psalmist and "do not act according to Your law," illustrating how pride diverts from obedience to God.
4. It is a disposition of the heart, a character of presumption that leads to acting without fear of God or respect for the limits imposed by His authority.
H2086.origine: The Hebrew word זֵד (zed) comes from a root that means "to boil," "to be in effervescence": the proud one is one whose heart "boils" with excessive pride. It is close to Hebrew verbs evoking agitation, insolence, and voluntary rebellion. This word fundamentally opposes the humility and submission that God expects from His servants.
H2086.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs, places where one meditates on justice and the fear of God. The context is always that of the conflict between the righteous and the insolent: the proud threaten, deceive, dig snares against the faithful (Psalms 119:69, 119:85). They stray from God's commandments (Psalms 119:21) and refuse to listen to His word (Jeremiah 43:2). God "threatens" them (Psalms 119:21) and announces that He will annihilate them (Isaiah 13:11; Malachi 4:1), showing that pride is incompatible with the reign of God.
H2086.portee: This word invites the believer to guard against pride, which is one of the roots of sin. In Psalms 19:14, the psalmist asks God to keep him from the proud, recognizing that arrogance is contagious and destructive. Understanding the fate of the proud in God's eyes — judgment and annihilation — encourages the believer towards humility and submission to His word, the only paths to blessing.

sens: Excessive and haughty pride towards others
Insolence, contempt for authority or wisdom
Presumptuous boldness, unjustified self-confidence
H2087.detail: 1. Pride is that inflated sense of self-importance that leads one to believe they are superior: it is the feeling of one's own importance taken to excess. When Eliab accuses David of his "pride" (1 Samuel 17:28), he accuses him of claiming more than he deserves, driven by a malicious heart seeking glory rather than service. It is also the trait of the scoffer in Proverbs 21:24, who "acts with the fury of arrogance." 2. Pride becomes insolence when it refuses to submit to established order: one who "by pride" does not listen to the judge sent by God (Deuteronomy 17:12) rejects legitimate authority with contempt. It is to push away the wisdom of others, as Proverbs 13:10 highlights: "It is only by pride that quarrels arise." 3. Presumptuous boldness is the self-confidence that exceeds reasonable limits: the false prophet who speaks "with boldness" (Deuteronomy 18:22) invents unfounded words, certain of his authority. Proverbs 11:2 reminds us that "when pride comes, disgrace follows" — the downfall that always follows this folly.
H2087.origine: The Hebrew word zadon comes from a root expressing the idea of "boiling" or "rising up." It literally describes what rises, swells, overflows — an image of this excess of pride that can no longer be contained. It is mainly found in Proverbs and in the oracles of judgment against proud nations (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Obadiah), where it characterizes the sin that provokes downfall.
H2087.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always with a connotation of condemnation. It is particularly frequent in Proverbs, where it stands in opposition to wisdom and humility: pride provokes quarrels (Proverbs 13:10), leads to shame (Proverbs 11:2), and characterizes the scoffer (Proverbs 21:24). It is also found in the laws of Deuteronomy to describe the refusal to respect authorities established by God. In the prophecies against the nations (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Obadiah), it denotes the arrogance of powers that believe themselves invulnerable and thus deserve divine judgment. The text of 1 Samuel 17:28 shows pride as a personal flaw, the fruit of a "malicious heart."
H2087.portee: Pride is presented by the Bible as the fundamental sin, the refusal to recognize God and the order He establishes. This word challenges every believer: are we among those who listen to legitimate wisdom and authority, or do we allow ourselves to be inflated by the certainty of our own judgment? The constant opposition between pride and humility in Proverbs shows that true strength does not come from pride, but from listening and submission to God.

sens: This, that, these (demonstrative adjective indicating something close)
Here is (introducing what follows)
That (neuter pronoun designating a thing, situation, or idea)
This one (pronoun designating a specific person or thing)
To be, to exist (functioning as a copula, expressing identity or existence)
Then, at that moment (marking the progression of the narrative)
H2088.detail: 1. This designates something close, as if by a hand gesture: "this people" (Exodus 32:9), "this book" (Deuteronomy 29:20). It is the most common demonstrative adjective in Hebrew, pointing to a particular person or thing. 2. Here is introduces what comes or what happens: "Here is the book of the descendants of Adam" (Genesis 5:1) announces the content that follows. It is a lively way to draw the reader's attention. 3. That designates a whole reality, a situation, or what has just happened: "that happened" condenses an action or event into a single thing. 4. This one isolates a person or thing among others: "this one... that one" establishes a clear distinction between two people or two things. 5. To be functions as a linking verb when זֶה connects two ideas: "it is a people" (Exodus 32:9) signifies the identity or nature of something. 6. Then marks the sequence of events, especially in poetry or narrative: the word punctuates the narration and creates fluidity in the timeline of the story.
H2088.origine: זֶה comes from an ancient Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pointing out, designating directly. Close roots are found in other Semitic languages, all related to this primary notion of pointing towards something visible and specific. It is a very archaic demonstrative, probably derived from a hand gesture that became a word. Like all demonstratives, זֶה creates proximity: not only is the object shown, but it is shown as close to the speaker.
H2088.emploi: זֶה is the most frequent Hebrew word for designating something close: it appears more than a thousand times in the Old Testament, in all books and in all contexts. In Genesis, it constantly appears to present events ("Here is the book", 5:1; "Here comes to you", 15:4) or to distinguish two things ("this one... that one", 25:32; 44:5). In speeches, זֶה emphasizes the importance of what is being discussed: "this people" (Exodus 32:9), "this thing" (Ezra 10:5). The word also functions as a linking verb to express identity: "it is a stiff-necked people." Finally, in narrative context, זֶה can mark the progression of time or simply draw attention to what is coming.
H2088.portee: This small, omnipresent word teaches us the importance of detail and proximity in God's word. The Bible never speaks in abstract: it shows, it designates, it brings close. When God says "here is," He invites us to look, to be attentive. This reminds us that God addresses us directly, personally, by showing us concrete realities: this people, this book, this covenant. It is a lesson in presence and clarity: the divine word is never distant or vague.

sens: what is present or close in space or time
what has just been said or designated
what is the subject of reflection or judgment
H2090.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what is within sight or thought, here and now. In 2 Kings 6:19, Elisha tells the Syrians, "This is not the way, and this is not the city": he points to what surrounds them, what they have under their eyes, the immediate present. 2. It also refers to what has just been mentioned or experienced, what is fresh in memory. In Ecclesiastes 2:24, the Preacher lists the pleasures of eating and drinking, then adds, "but I have seen that this also comes from the hand of God": this refers back to everything that precedes. 3. Finally, it is used to show the object of a moral and spiritual judgment or evaluation. In Ecclesiastes 5:15, in the face of the vanity of accumulating wealth, the wise man says, "This is still a serious evil": this designates the human condition he has just painted and condemns.
H2090.origine: The Hebrew word זֹה comes from the root זה, which expresses demonstrating, indicating by pointing. It belongs to the family of Hebrew demonstratives and is used to point to what is present or to refer back to what is known. In the Greek Old Testament, it often corresponds to Greek terms like τοῦτο (touto) or ὁ (ho) that play the same role of demonstration or anaphora.
H2090.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the provided biblical text, concentrated notably in Ecclesiastes. It is used consistently to point to what is immediately present or known: in 2 Samuel 11:25, "sometimes one, sometimes the other" (where זֹה replaces the pronoun in repetition); in 2 Kings 6:19, "here" marks the place where one is; in Ecclesiastes, where it is the favorite instrument of the wise to traverse the vanity of the world and designate what comes from God. Translations vary ("that", "there", "here") depending on the context, but always to refer back to or show what is at hand.
H2090.portee: For the Christian reader, this small word helps to understand how the Bible speaks of what is present and accessible. Particularly in Ecclesiastes, its repeated use forces one to see that ordinary life — eating, drinking, working — is what we have at hand, and that it is precisely there that God acts and speaks to us. It is a lesson in attention to the present and gratitude for the concrete gift of God here and now.

sens: precious and shiny metal, highly valued in antiquity
weight used to weigh and measure precious metals
wealth, splendor, and radiant beauty
excellence and moral purity
H2091.detail:
1. Gold is a highly valued precious metal with a remarkable golden luster. In the Bible, it is among the most coveted treasures: Abraham possessed much of it (Genesis 13:2), and the king of Syria sent ten talents of gold to Samaria as a royal gift (2 Kings 5:5).
2. Gold was also used as a standard of weight. The quantity of gold was measured in "shekels," a unit of mass: Gideon requested one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold as his share of the spoils (Judges 8:26).
3. Gold symbolizes splendor and radiant beauty. In the tabernacle, God commands that the sacred furniture be made of gold or overlaid with gold: the Ark of the Covenant, the lampstand, the table, the altar (Exodus 25 and 37), thus expressing the holiness and majesty of His dwelling.
4. Figuratively, gold represents moral value, purity, and spiritual excellence: what is true, authentic, and precious in the eyes of God is worth more than all the gold in the world.
H2091.origine: The Hebrew word zaḥav (זָהָב) etymologically denotes what shines and gleams. In Aramaic, the parallel form is deḥav (דְּהַב), found in the Aramaic passages of Daniel. The word belongs to the family of precious metals; it is related to roots evoking brightness and light, as gold was the most precious and luminous of the metals known to the Hebrews.
H2091.emploi: The word "gold" appears 336 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Exodus, where it dominates the descriptions of the tabernacle and its sacred furnishings. It is also found in the accounts of patriarchal wealth (Genesis), in royal histories as a testimony of prestige (2 Kings, 2 Chronicles), and in wisdom sayings. Gold can refer to raw metal brought as an offering (Exodus 35:22), worked gold shaped into ritual objects (Exodus 37), or gold assessed by weight (Numbers 7:14: ten shekels of pure gold). Its usage systematically blends literal meaning (the material) and figurative meaning (value, divine splendor).
H2091.portee: For the believer, gold in the Bible is not merely an object of desire but a sign of God's magnificence. Seeing the tabernacle adorned with gold reminds us that God deserves the finest gifts. At the same time, passages that warn against the love of gold (such as the worship of the golden calf, Exodus 32) invite us not to confuse earthly wealth with true spiritual value. Gold thus reflects the biblical tension between honoring God through beauty and not worshiping riches.

sens: To experience intense repulsion, aversion
To find something repugnant, abominable
H2092.detail:
1. The word evokes a feeling of deep repulsion towards something considered filthy or disgusting. It is a mix of physical and moral disgust: one no longer wants to see or touch it. In Job 33:20, it is the illness that makes the sick person loathe food, even the most appetizing, so much that their body revolts and rejects all nourishment.
2. More broadly, it means to find something so abominable that one pushes it far away. It is the feeling of someone who looks at something or someone as repugnant, unworthy of being approached.
H2092.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of dirtiness, impurity. The form used here (the Piel) intensifies the meaning, as if saying "to make loathsome" or "to cause to become disgusting." The word belongs to the lexical field of purity and impurity, which is omnipresent in the Hebrew Bible: what is filthy naturally provokes disgust.
H2092.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 33:20. It is used to describe the sick person's loathing of food during their illness. Even the most delicious dishes become repugnant when the body suffers and revolts. It is an example of biblical language at extremes: a suffering so intense that it overturns the natural order of things (one should love good bread, but illness makes it disgusting).
H2092.portee: This word reminds us that illness affects a person in their entirety: not only does the body deteriorate, but the soul does as well, to the point that even ordinary joys become impossible. It invites us to compensate for the suffering of the sick with special attention and compassion.

sens: Son of King Rehoboam and Mahalath
H2093.detail: Zaham is a prince of Judah, the son of King Rehoboam and his wife Mahalath, who was herself the granddaughter of King David. He appears only once in the Bible, listed among the sons that Rehoboam had with Mahalath, alongside his brothers Jeusch and Schemaria. He is a minor character from the time of the Divided Monarchy, with no further mention or events reported about him.
H2093.origine: The name means "disgust" or "repugnance" in Hebrew, evoking a reaction of rejection or loathing. His father, Rehoboam, was the son of Solomon and the first king of Judah after the schism of the united kingdom.
H2093.emploi: Zaham is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Chronicles 11:19, where he is cited as one of the sons of Rehoboam and Mahalath. No particular event is associated with him in the biblical text. His mention is part of a genealogical enumeration intended to document the royal lineage of Judah during the period of the Divided Monarchy.

sens: To emit light, to radiate
To be luminous, brilliant
Figuratively: to stand out by one's brilliance, excellence
H2094A.detail: 1. The verb first describes the physical action of emitting light or radiating — it is the image of the sun, stars, or any surface that reflects light and shines. 2. It then evokes the state of being luminous, brilliant, radiant, like something that naturally shines. 3. In the Bible, this meaning is transposed figuratively to speak of moral or spiritual excellence that "shows": the one who shines is the one who stands out, who excels. In Daniel 12:3, the wise and the righteous "will shine" like the heavens and the stars — their wisdom and faithfulness will make them visible and admirable forever, like permanent stars in the sky.
H2094A.origine: The verb zahar comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally expresses the idea of light and clarity. Its starting image is that of light manifesting, appearing: to shine is to become visible through light. The form used in Daniel (the Hiphil) reinforces this meaning by emphasizing the action of emitting, actively producing this light or brilliance.
H2094A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 12:3. It is an eschatological passage, where the prophet speaks of the final time and resurrection. The righteous and the wise are promised a glorious destiny: they will shine forever like the stars of heaven. This context shows how Scripture uses this rare verb to express not only physical light but especially future glory, the visible and perpetual reward of those who have sought justice and wisdom.
H2094A.portee: This word invites the reader to see their faithfulness and righteousness not as isolated acts, but as a light that will shine forever. It promises that the one who walks in God's wisdom will not fade into oblivion: their work will shine eternally, visible like the stars. It is a powerful encouragement to persevere in righteousness even when the world seems dark.

sens: To give a warning, to caution
To instruct, to teach a doctrine or a rule
To pay attention, to be on guard
H2094B.detail:
1. To warn means to inform someone of an imminent danger or threat, so that they can protect themselves or change their behavior. This is the role of the sentinel established by God: they will "warn" the people when the sword approaches (Ezekiel 33:4). Those who hear this warning and do not heed it will bear the consequences (Ezekiel 33:4).
2. To teach means to convey knowledge, a directive, or a law so that the people know how to live. Moses must "teach" the Israelites the ordinances and laws (Exodus 18:20), showing them the way they should follow.
3. To receive instruction or warning means to be willing to learn and benefit from it. Psalm 19:12 speaks of one who "receives instruction" by observing God's commandments, and a great reward awaits them.
4. To turn someone away means to stop them before they commit evil, by warning them of the consequences. If a righteous person turns away from their righteousness and they have not been "warned," they will die, and their death will be charged to the one who should have warned them (Ezekiel 3:20).
H2094B.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that initially evokes the idea of "shining," "illuminating" — hence the image of light that reveals danger. In Aramaic, the corresponding form (זְהַר) means "to pay attention." The verb can be used in a passive sense ("to be taught, to be admonished") or in an active causative sense ("to teach, to warn"), which shows how the warning passes from one person to another to enlighten and protect.
H2094B.emploi: This verb appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Ezekiel and the Psalms. Ezekiel is its primary user: the prophet is established as a sentinel and must warn the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3:17; 33:7). Each warning has a vital stake: whoever does not heed the warning perishes, and the one responsible for the warning may be held accountable (Ezekiel 3:20; 33:4). In other contexts, the word refers to the teaching of laws (Exodus 18:20) or the instruction derived from observing the commandments (Psalms 19:12). The meaning remains constant: it is always about communicating a truth intended to protect or edify.
H2094B.portee: This word reminds the reader that God provides to warn His people through prophets and teachers, and that receiving this warning or teaching is a grace. It also invites not to ignore spiritual warnings, as negligence can lead to death. For the one who teaches or warns, this word emphasizes a serious responsibility: to communicate faithfully the word of God, knowing that the fate of others depends on it.

sens: To pay attention, to be on guard
To avoid a danger or evil by being vigilant
To abstain from something out of caution
H2095.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of taking heed, meaning to be attentive and aware of a risk or threat. In Ezra 4:22, the king advises the governors to take heed — to be careful — not to be negligent in carrying out his orders, or else disorder would worsen.
2. It involves active vigilance that drives one to avoid evil or danger. This caution may be motivated by fear of negative consequences: here, the king asks for attention so that evil does not increase.
3. By extension, to take heed means to voluntarily abstain from an action or negligence. It is a call to discipline and responsibility: not to let negligence gain ground.
H2095.origine: The Hebrew verb זְהַר (zehar) expresses the idea of shining or being luminous at its origin, then developed to mean "to be attentive" or "to take heed" — as if vigilance were a light that illuminates dangers. The root belongs to the family of verbs of attention and caution, very present in biblical Hebrew to express wisdom and the fear of the Lord.
H2095.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:22. It is used in a royal decree where King Artaxerxes asks the governors to take heed, meaning to remain vigilant and attentive to the execution of his decrees. The context is political and administrative: it is about maintaining order and avoiding negligence that could have serious consequences. The word emphasizes the importance of vigilance and personal responsibility.
H2095.portee: This word reminds the believer of the necessity to remain vigilant against spiritual and moral dangers. Taking heed is a form of practical wisdom: it requires conscious attention to risks and a willingness to avoid evil. In a time of distraction and laxity, the call to take heed invites discipline and personal responsibility in the life of faith.

sens: A bright light that shines and dazzles
The luminous radiance of a polished or precious surface
Glory and splendor that radiate from a person or a divine reality
H2096.detail:
1. Brightness is primarily an intense and brilliant light, one that dazzles the eye — like when looking at polished bronze in the sun. Ezekiel sees the upper part of the heavenly figure shining with a brightness like polished bronze (Ezekiel 8:2), a clarity so vivid that it impresses and captivates the seer.
2. The word also denotes the radiance of a well-polished surface, which reflects light strongly — it is the image of bronze or metal that shines. This material brightness suggests purity and perfection.
3. Figuratively, brightness becomes the glory and splendor that emanate from a person, especially when they participate in the divine reality. Those who have been wise and have taught righteousness will shine with a heavenly brightness, like the stars (Daniel 12:3): their brightness expresses their dignity and their participation in eternal glory.
H2096.origine: The Hebrew word zohar comes from a root that means "to be bright" or "to shine." It evokes the concrete image of light that bursts forth and radiates, which one sees on a polished surface. It is a rare word in the Old Testament, used mainly in prophetic visions to describe the supernatural clarity that accompanies divine or heavenly appearances.
H2096.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first time in Ezekiel, the prophet uses "brightness" to describe the upper part of a resplendent heavenly figure he sees in vision — a detail that underscores the supernatural and impressive nature of the vision. The second occurrence is found in Daniel, where brightness becomes a future reward: those who have shown wisdom and taught righteousness will shine with eternal splendor like the stars of heaven. In both cases, the word paints the beauty and glory that radiate from a transcendent reality.
H2096.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that divine glory is dazzling and visible, that it radiates and attracts. It also helps us understand that our participation in future glory will have something of this heavenly brightness: those who have been faithful and righteous will shine with eternal clarity. It is a promise of transformation and dignity for the people of God.

sens: what is at stake, what is in question
what characterizes or defines something
what draws attention
H2097.detail:
1. The word simply designates what is being talked about: what has just been mentioned or what is before the eyes of the listener. In Psalms 132:12, "their sons" will observe the covenant and "that" — the promise that their sons will sit on the throne — will be fulfilled forever.
2. It can also mark what defines something or characterizes a situation. In Hosea 7:16, Israel's rebellion against God and especially "that" — the insolence of their tongue, this particular trait — will make them an object of ridicule in Egypt: it is this specific fact that will lead to this consequence.
H2097.origine: This demonstrative pronoun belongs to the stock of basic pronouns in biblical Hebrew. It comes from a root that refers to the idea of showing or pointing out: like all demonstratives, it serves to point out, to highlight what matters. It is a simple and direct tool of everyday language, without particular nuance.
H2097.emploi: The pronoun appears only twice in the preserved biblical texts. First in Psalms 132:12, where it refers to the divine promise concerning David's royal lineage. Then in Hosea 7:16, where it designates the insolence of Israel's tongue — that is, verbal rebellion, the pride of the people — as the cause of their humiliation. In both cases, the word links an action or a quality to its consequences or realizations.
H2097.portee: This little word reminds us that the biblical word always points to something concrete and relevant. When God promises or when the prophet warns, what is at stake — "that" — is never vague or abstract: it is a precise reality that engages our responsibility and obedience.

sens: What is close or present before the speaker or listener
What has just been named or spoken about
This one (to designate a person)
The way, the path, the direction (in expressions like 'the way you should follow')
H2098.detail:
1. This word designates what is immediately present or close: it points to something, so to speak. In Exodus 15:13, "this people" refers to the Israelites just mentioned, present in mind as a concrete group.
2. It refers back to what has just been named to return to it or explain it further. In Psalms 9:16, "the net they have hidden" relies on this net mentioned just before: the word shows that we are talking about the same net, the one that the wicked have prepared.
3. It can demonstratively designate a person: "this one" or "this one". It is a common means in Hebrew to point to someone or something.
4. In phrases like Psalms 32:8 and Psalms 143:8 ("the way you should follow"), it links a general idea to its precise application: that path, the one you need right now.
H2098.origine: זוּ (zu) is an ancient Hebrew demonstrative pronoun, related to other pronouns in the same family (זֶה zeH, "this one"). Its basic image is that of a finger pointing: it has no abstract meaning, but always a sense of concrete designation. It comes from a very ancient root common to Semitic languages, where it expresses the act of showing or indicating.
H2098.emploi: זוּ (zu) appears fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and prophetic books. It functions as a relative or demonstrative pronoun: sometimes it refers back to a name just mentioned ("the people" in Exodus 15:13, "the net" in Psalms 9:16), sometimes it introduces a restriction or precision ("the way you should follow" in Psalms 32:8). In Psalms 143:8, it links the general request ("make me know") to a precise necessity (that path, the path of my present life). Its use is discreet but constant: it creates coherence in discourse by linking what is said to what has been said or what is being talked about.
H2098.portee: This little word teaches the reader that biblical prayer is never vague or purely general: it always points to the concrete, to what I am experiencing now. When the psalmist asks God to show him "the way I should follow," it is not an abstract path; it is my life, my decision, my road today. The demonstrative pronoun anchors faith in the present and the particular.

sens: Second month of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to April-May
H2099.detail: 1. Ziv is the name of the second month of the year in the ancient Hebrew calendar. Its name means "brightness" or "glory" in Hebrew, evoking the brightness and blooming of spring. The Bible mentions it during the construction of the temple by Solomon: "in the month of Ziv, which is the second month" (1 Kings 6:1). It was during this time that Solomon began the work, in the fourth year of his reign, and the foundations were laid (1 Kings 6:37).
H2099.origine: The word Ziv comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." This month name evokes the image of spring in the Holy Land, a time of increasing clarity and plant renewal. Unlike simply numbered months ("first month," "third month"), Ziv carries a poetic name that reflects the beauty of this season.
H2099.emploi: Ziv appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the context of the construction of the temple by Solomon (1 Kings 6:1 and 6:37). These two verses indicate that it was in the month of Ziv in the fourth year of Solomon's reign that this major construction began. The Hebrew calendar had several dating systems: the religious system began in the month of Nisan (the first month), while Ziv was the second month in this order. This month became particularly memorable for the faith of Israel as it marked the beginning of the construction of the holy place intended to house the ark of the covenant.
H2099.portee: The month of Ziv reminds the reader that the Bible situates the great events of sacred history within a concrete and observed calendar: God acts in the real time of His people. The construction of the temple, a major event for Israel's worship, is thus inscribed in a calendar marked by the rhythms of nature and the seasons that God has created. This shows that the unfolding of the history of salvation respects a divine order, measured and certain.
